author_response_spans.text: ## **Response to Reviewers**
## **Paper Title: “Optical Tweezing of Microparticles and Cells Using Silicon-Photonics-Based Optical Phased Arrays” Revised Paper,** _**Nature Communications**_ **(Manuscript ID NCOMMS-23-19192)**

This paper (Manuscript ID NCOMMS-23-19192) was submitted to _Nature Communications_ . After an initial review, the editor provided comments from the reviewers and gave us an opportunity to address the comments and revise the manuscript.

We sincerely appreciate the comments, as they have helped us clarify and further improve the manuscript, as specified in this document. In this document, we provide all the comments from the reviewers and our responses to these comments (reviewers’ comments are given in **blue** and our responses are in **black** ). All **changes are tracked** in the revised manuscript and are referenced and explained in this document.
## **Response to Comments from Reviewer 1:**

In this manuscript, the authors report the use of an OPA to demonstrate optical tweezing and trapping and show that the standoff distance is increased significantly. The manuscript is well-written and would be of interest to other scientists and engineers and I recommend publication in Nature Communications. I think it would make the paper stronger if my comments and questions below are addressed.
**Reviewer 1, Comment 1:** Since grating based antennas are used, it would be useful for the authors to discuss the level of laser wavelength stability needed for the intended application.

**Reviewer 1, Response 1:** Indeed, a discussion of required stability of the laser coupled to the system is important for integrated photonics systems, as it places constraints on the types of lasers that can be used with the system in commercial settings, including low-cost co-packaged diode lasers. For small wavelength changes, the relationship between wavelength and focal position is essentially linear; from this, we can extrapolate that, for an example target position stability of one micron, equivalent to the position stability of a trapped bead at around 30 mW input power, we would need a wavelength stability of 64.5pm. This is nearly two orders of magnitude larger than the laser stability of the benchtop lasers used in our lab, demonstrating that our device is not particularly sensitive to the stability of the input laser. A brief discussion on this point has been added to Page 5 of the revised manuscript:

“Common scientific benchtop lasers, such as the Agilent systems used in this work, offer wavelength step sizes and stabilities in the range of a few picometers, corresponding to theoretical spot position variation in the tens of nanometers; this is significantly smaller than the position variation of a trapped particle due to random motion for the trap powers under study.”

Ultimately, the final application will determine the required laser stability; biophysics experiments will require much higher position stability than sorting or diagnostic applications. The integrated photonic system presented in this work is flexible for both sorts of target usages; the determining factor here will be the quality of laser that is coupled into the system.
**Reviewer 1, Comment 2:** What phase adjustment resolution is needed for precise tweezer control?

**Reviewer 1, Response 2:** For our OPA-based architecture, the phase adjustment resolution in the array dimension will primarily affect the quality of the spot, both in terms of shape and beam waist, as opposed to its position, which would be the result of consistent phase errors across the array. This note has been added to Page 4 of the manuscript:
“Note that errors in the encoded phase due to fabrication variations will present themselves primarily as a degradation in the resulting spot quality and expansion of the beam waist.”

**Reviewer 1, Comment 3:** The authors should discuss the OPA calibration (and focal point distortion correction). What is the effect of the pitch of the elements being larger than wavelength (on the focusing the light into the focal point)?

**Reviewer 1, Response 3:** Both of the above points raise important discussion on the ways in which our group designed the phased array to mitigate the impacts of fabrication variations and undesired crosscoupling between antenna elements. This particular device, as a first proof-of-concept demonstration, was designed to be passive, without heater-based active tuning elements which allow for phase calibration after fabrication but also add significant complexity to system operation and packaging. In order to reduce dependence on calibration, phase was imparted using adiabatic phase bumps, which were designed to be relatively fabrication-tolerant for the range of phases required for the system. The effectiveness of this fabrication-aware design is borne out in the experimental beam profile, which is both largely uniform and close to its theoretical diffraction-limited dimensions, as noted on Page 5 of the manuscript:

“The fabricated system focuses tightly at the designed focal height of 5 mm, with a power full-width halfmaximum (FWHM) of approximately 6.4 µm along the array dimension and 7.6 µm along the antenna dimension, closely matching the expected FWHM of 6.6 µm x 7.6 µm from simulation [23].”

Regarding the second point, the use of an array spacing larger than λ/2, while reducing undesired cross-coupling between antenna elements, introduces additional grating lobes. However, since these lobes are at a relatively large angle, they are far out of both the field of view and focal plane of experimentation, and thus their main impact on the system is reducing efficiency by drawing power from the main radiation lobe (see figure below that shows the simulated emission pattern). Subwavelength grating spacing can be explored as part of future work, and is particularly interesting as part of systems which have more complex holographic patterns encoded into them, such as arrays of optical traps, where the additional element density will improve the fidelity of the emission profile. A note on this point has been added to the revised manuscript on Page 4:

“Since the antennas are spaced with an antenna pitch larger than λ/2, the system also generates higher-order grating lobes in the array dimension; however, these lobes appear at larger angles and are far out of both the field of view and focal plane of experimentation, and, consequently, their main impact on the system is only reducing efficiency by drawing power from the main lobe.”

**Reviewer 1, Comment 4:** In Fig. 3(b), it would be useful to see if the motion of the microspheres that are not within the trap follows the expected Brownian motion model (within the monitored 75 second).

**Reviewer 1, Response 4:** In the case of Fig. 3(b), the particles in this image and many other experiments done around the same time exhibited both Brownian motion and a weak directional flow. When samples were left on the setup and studied for some time, they slowly began to dry out from their input opening, causing a flow in that direction. This drying gave a directionality to the random motion that can be seen in the untrapped microspheres in Fig. 3(b).

While the motion observed in the qualitative results features this flow in addition to random motion, in our quantitative results, such as in Fig. 3(d), the motion is almost entirely Brownian. The reason for this is that, in order to perform accurate repeats with appropriate variable control, each sample was imaged directly after preparation and then discarded. At these time scales, appreciable drying did not occur, and the beads’ motion appears as the classic Brownian motion, without the influence of an external flow. A clarification to this point is added in the manuscript on Page 6:

“The two freely-moving spheres exhibit movement largely under the influence of Brownian motion, with the additional influence of a directional fluid flow caused by evaporation of the sample from one of its edges.”
**Reviewer 1, Comment 5:** What is the effect of the laser stability on the maximum speed of the tweezer movement (before the microspheres fall out of the trap)?

**Reviewer 1, Response 5:** As discussed in **Reviewer 1, Response 1** , the required laser stability for the trap to remain more stable than the random position fluctuations of the trapped object under the input power of 44.4 mW used in the steering experiments is around 50pm, which does not pose a challenge to benchtop laser systems. For applications where a lower cost or significantly smaller laser is desired, we would expect that these fluctuations could start to affect the maximum speed of tweezing. This is particularly relevant for lasers without temperature stabilization circuitry, since short timescale fluctuations are expected to have less of an impact given the speed at which the bead tweezes, while temperature drift could more seriously affect the fidelity and range of tweezing versus expected performance. A note on this was added to the revised manuscript on Page 5:

“For applications where less precision is required, lower-cost laser diodes can also be used with the OPA optical tweezers; however, if temperature stabilization circuitry is not included with the laser, wavelength stability will begin to have a noticeable effect on the stiffness and maximum force of the trap.”
## **Response to Comments from Reviewer 2:**

In this article the reviewers demonstrate a neat application of an optical phased array (OPA) incorporated into a silicon based photonic chip. By imposing a hyperbolic phase variation across the attennas comprising the OPA, a focus can be formed, in the array dimension, above the chip (5 mm above). Tuning the period of the grating-based antennas provides focusing in the orthogonal direction, apparently forming an optical trap. Varying the input wavelength modifies the Bragg condition allowing the focal spot to be shifted along the array dimension. The authors provide demonstrations of optical trapping and tweezing of dielectric microspheres and successfully manipulate a biological cell which deforms as it is dragged by the trap.

To start with, I should point out that I am primarily a theoretical physicist - with a strong interest in optical forces, structured light and photonics (including integrated photonics) in general, as well as stochastic thermodynamics and biophysics. Thus my experience is, perhaps, only tangentially relevant to this paper. However, I collaborate pretty continuously with experimentalists working in these fields and have done so for many years and so I think I have a reasonably broad overview of the relevant science.

My overall impression of this article is that it is not suitable for a high IF journal like Nat. Comms. but is, without doubt, suitable for a more technical journal, particularly one with a focus on instrumentation. The reason for this assessment is connected with the significance of the work, as described below, not the legitimacy or validity of the results. Indeed, I think this is a valuable contribution to the literature and may (possibly) have useful applications - the authors should be congratulated for this. Below I summarize my assemement of the significance of the work, make some minor scientific criticisms and suggest potential ways of strengthening the work.
## SIGNIFICANCE

The significance of this work derives from the significance of the instrument the authors have developed and on the useful applications that it enables especially those that have been demonstrated in the article. My judgement is the work falls short in both categories.

**Reviewer 2, Comment 1:** To start with the instrument. First, I agree that this is a neat and novel application of an integrated OPA. However, as I'm sure the authors would conceded, it does not do anything which cannot be done more precisely and flexibably with bulk optics, for example, by using a digital micromirror device, or similar. The virtues of this instrument lie, therefore, not on the uniqueness of its fundamental capabilities but on its cost, or on high-throuput applications.

**Reviewer 2, Response 1:** Indeed, as with most integrated optical systems, a large bulk optical system will usually perform more strongly in several key metrics. However, the advantages in cost, form-factor, complexity of operation, and mass producibility, among others, are critical to the significance of the work. As a result, silicon photonics systems, ranging from LiDAR to optical transducers, have been widely published in high-impact journals and seen significant success in garnering seed funding for start-ups, and specifically implementations of integrated optical tweezers have been published throughout the years in Nature portfolio journals [11,13,14].

In the specific case of bulk optical tweezers, the cost, size, and complexity of operation of these tools have limited their broader accessibility, especially to biology labs which lack the infrastructure or expertise to operate complex optical research tools but often have insight into some of the most interesting questions that these tools can be used to answer. This is one of the central reasons we chose to submit to _Nature Communications_ as opposed to more technical optics journals, which are less likely to be read by researchers from such labs. The aforementioned points are mentioned in the manuscript on Page 1: “However, since standard optical tweezers consist of benchtop systems comprised of bulk-optical components, their cost, complexity, and need for specialized laboratory equipment have limited broad access to these standard bulk-optical tweezers.”

As it stands, however, there are critical gaps in the performance of these systems. In Ye et. al [11], published in _Nature Communications_ , the authors address one such gap, maximum trap force. In this work, we address standoff distance, a critical factor to ensure compatibility with existing experimental techniques that has until now severely limited the application space to which integrated optical tweezers can be applied. This is discussed in more depth on Page 2 of the manuscript:

“While these systems offer significant advantages in form factor and complexity compared to standard bulk-optical systems, they have been restricted to trapping either directly on or within several microns from the surface of the chip (Fig. 1(b)). This significantly limits their widespread applicability in biophysics and cell experimentation, which typically involve sterile glass coverslips or cell culture wells that are at least 150 µm thick, since their focal heights are too short to penetrate into these standard sample chambers. Without the ability to use these ubiquitous methods of sample preparation, these prior integrated optical tweezers could only be used in a narrow set of experiments, such as with back-end-of-the-line microfluidics fabricated on top of the chips, which require additional time to fabricate, often necessitate disposal of the chip after each experiment due to contamination, and are non-sterile surfaces that are not compatible with the majority of biophysics, and especially cell, research. As such, extending standoff

distances to the millimeter scale to enable compatibility with these standard sample-preparation methods is an important requirement for integrated optical tweezers to become a practical technology (and could even enable demonstrations in emerging _in-vivo_ tweezing applications that require millimeter-scale standoff distances [7]).”

Throughout this response, we want to highlight that it was not our intention that the potential application of high-throughput sorting stick out in particular to readers, and in several of the following comments (and especially in **Reviewer 2, Response 3** ) reference changes made in the manuscript to clarify and minimize this specific point. While OPA’s can be used to holographically encode arrays of traps as discussed in **Reviewer 3, Response 3** , our original intention was to mention that the mass-producibility of these integrated traps, produced using traditional silicon microelectronics fabrication processes, allows them to be “copy-pasted” many times over within a small area and be used, for example, in highlymultiplexed devices. This specific application of high-throughput sorting is not a critical part of the manuscript, and we’ve made several edits to clarify as such.
**Reviewer 2, Comment 2:** However, (i) this approach uses a tunable laser to steer the beams in 1 dimension - and tunable lasers with the required specs. are not cheap, and,

**Reviewer 2, Response 2:** The OPA-based system is tested in this work with a relatively high-end laser in order to maximize reproducibility and explore the capabilities of the device, but it is important to differentiate between the system itself and the laser attached to it, which can be exchanged depending on the demands of the experiment at hand. We agree that this was insufficiently addressed in the original manuscript, and needs to be discussed in-depth in the text, particularly given the wider readership of _Nature Communications_ , in order to make clearer the impact of the system. This has been addressed through a number of edits in the manuscript, as described throughout this response.

On Page 5, we indicate that the laser is an interchangeable part of the system: “To characterize the fabricated system, we utilize an Agilent 81600B tunable benchtop laser source and an optical system to image…”

The challenge of reducing laser cost can be met in three different ways. Firstly, our system’s current requirement for a C-band laser with a 1-2nm tuning range can be readily fulfilled with inexpensive thermally-tuned laser systems. This will naturally entail tradeoffs between cost and linewidth or wavelength stability, which will in turn degrade the performance of the trap.

Secondly, there is a growing body of literature on integrated laser systems, including tunable ones (see P. A. Morton et. al, “Integrated Coherent Tunable Laser (ICTL) With Ultra-Wideband Wavelength Tuning and Sub-100 Hz Lorentzian Linewidth,” APL Photonics (2022)). In the future, we could realize integrated optical tweezers in their entirety on chip, without the need for an external laser. A discussion on both of these points is now included in the revised manuscript on Page 9: “Although these experiments were performed with a benchtop tunable laser in order to accurately characterize the system and maximize repeatability, this functionality and wavelength tuning range could be readily achieved by powering the system using an inexpensive laser diode with thermal tuning or even an on-chip integrated tunable laser on the same photonic chip [30, 31].”

Finally, and by far the most interesting from our point of view, is the addition of active tuning to the system. In future work, we hope to control the trap position in three dimensions, using electrical signals as opposed to wavelength steering. While this adds control complexity and poses a significant system architecture challenge, it will allow the system to operate with an inexpensive co-packaged singlewavelength diode laser and expands the utility of the device by enabling more degrees of freedom for movement of the trap. This is clarified on Page 11 of the revised manuscript:

“Third, novel focusing OPA architectures that incorporate electro-optic or thermo-optic modulators could be developed that enable non-mechanical two- or three-dimensional steering of the focal spot and do not require a tunable laser source [23].”

**Reviewer 2, Comment 3:** (ii) the authors have not demonstrated the scalability of the approach either in its own terms or in comparison to conventional holographic optical traps (HOTs)- in contrast, it is routine to independently control multiple traps with holography. One very recent article ("Rapid tilted-plane Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm for holographic optical tweezers", Yanan Cai et al, Optics Express (2020)) demonstrated simultaneous trapping and manipulation of a 7 by 7 array of beads - I have seen still greater feats of parallel manipulation myself. The point is - if the authors wish to claim that their device is capable of very high throughput studies or assays, then I think this needs to be demonstrated to some degree. It should, for instance, be relatively trivial to outperform existing techniques in this respect. A demonstration of the simultaneous manipulation of 100s of particles, say, would be impressive.

**Reviewer 2, Response 3:** As mentioned in **Reviewer 2, Response 1** , we want to de-emphasize the potential for high-throughput applications, as this is not intended as a primary focus for the reader. The major significance of the device does not derive from its throughput; this is simply an example of an application for which integrated optical tweezers could be adapted. To this end, we have made several modifications in the revised manuscript:

On Page 1, high-throughput was changed to mass manufactured and broadly accessible: “Integrated optical tweezers have the potential to enable highly-compact, low-cost, mass-manufactured, and broadlyaccessible optical manipulation when compared to standard bulk-optical tweezers.”

On Page 3, the phrase high-throughput was removed from the following sentence: “Overall, this work introduces a new modality for integrated optical tweezers, significantly expanding the utility and compatibility of integrated tweezers with both common biological experiments and emerging in-vivo trapping research by extending their focal heights to the millimeter scale, with promising applications ranging from DNA and protein experiments to cell manipulation and sorting.”

On Page 12, high-throughput was changed to mass-producibility: “This OPA-based approach offers the advantages in cost, footprint, complexity, and mass producibility of integrated tweezers, while providing much of the functionality of bulk-optical systems.”
Increased trapping throughput as a potential application is now mentioned only very briefly in the manuscript.

While we do not want to highlight high-throughput as a target application, as discussed in **Reviewer 3, Response 3** , this is very much still a feasible extension of the system, and multiplexing multiple traps on the same chip or encoding arrays of traps holographically are very much of interest for future work. A note on this has been added to the revised manuscript on Page 11, along with a citation for Cai et al: “These future OPA architectures could also be designed to encode advanced holographic emission patterns of interest [45], such as closely-spaced arrays of traps for high-throughput trapping applications [32, 46].” However, realizing these designs would require another chip hardware tapeout with the CMOS fabrication foundry (requiring additional funding and a time scale of approximately a year) and therefore such demonstrations are outside of the scope of this paper.

**Reviewer 2, Comment 4:** Finally, (iii) the focal point generated by the OPA in this article is very weak compared with conventional optical trapping, for which beams are close to diffraction limited (i.e. beam waist radius comparable to half the wavelength). Although this may help when it comes to trapping the larger spheres and cells considered in this paper, the reported stiffnesses and drag rates remain low compared with those connected with HOT (e.g. this article reports stiffnesses of ~0.005 pN/micron - while stiffnesses of microspheres are often 10's of pN/micron). Connected with this, the reported drag rates are relatively low (e.g. Fig. 4 shows drag rates of ~10 microns in 100 seconds). These low stiffnesses and drag rates add to my questions about the scalability of this instrument. How much laser power would the authors expect to be required for manipulating, for example, the 49 spheres manipulated in the article by Cia et al, referred to above?

**Reviewer 2, Response 4:** The reviewer does raise an important point here. While the forces we generate here are sufficient to trap and manipulate objects of interest and are in line with other integrated optical

trapping demonstrations, they are significantly lower than the forces and trap stiffness of bulk-optical tweezers. We will address below various reasons why this is the case. It is important to note that lower trapping forces are largely not inherently a feature of OPA-based optical traps, and are largely a result of design trade-offs and the choice of laser used for characterization.

First, we want to mention that, for focusing from an aperture of size 1mm[2] to a focal height of 5mm, our focal spot is very close to diffraction limited for the aperture size. We have now highlighted this on Page 5 of the manuscript: “The fabricated system focuses tightly at the designed focal height of 5 mm, with a power full-width half-maximum (FWHM) of approximately 6.4 µm along the array dimension and 7.6 µm along the antenna dimension, closely matching the expected FWHM of 6.6 µm x 7.6 µm from simulation [23].”

With a different aperture size and focal height, the focal diameter can be reduced further, increasing the gradient force of the optical trap. The details behind this, as well as the design tradeoffs involved, are discussed in detail in **Reviewer 2, Response 8** . The limits on the minimum dimensions of the focal spot can be derived from the Rayleigh criterion, and will scale inversely with aperture size and linearly with focal height of OPA (as shown in the figure below). In this way, the FWHM can be significantly reduced by either increasing aperture size or decreasing focal height. A discussion of this has been added to Page 4 of the revised manuscript:

“The dimensions of the resulting focal spot, which impact the trapping efficiency, scale inversely with the OPA aperture size and linearly with the OPA focal height [23], allowing the characteristics of the system to be adjusted to fit the desired application. In this demonstration, we target polystyrene beads and cells with sizes around 10 µm. As a result, an aperture size of 1 mm2 and focal height of 5 mm were chosen to provide a reasonable tradeoff between trapping efficiency, focal height, and system footprint.”

It’s also worth clarifying that the laser powers we report throughout the paper are the power output from the laser, not the final power emitted from the trap itself. As mentioned on Page 5 of the revised manuscript, the trap power is around -12 dB down from the input power, or only about 1/16[th] of the input power. We feel that this is the most honest way to report the data. However, it is important to realize, when comparing to bulk-optical traps, the stiffness we report at 40 mW input power is expected to match more closely to those achieved in the (very low) 2-3 mW power range for bulk-optical traps (when we take into account the -12 dB drop). In addition, the 10-µm beads we use here have lower trapping stiffnesses than micron-sized beads. With these factors combined, our impression from the literature is that we could expect trapping stiffness in the 0.05-0.5 pN/µm range for bulk optical tweezers operating at similar output powers from the trap (see, for example, N. Malagnino et. al., “Measurements of trapping efficiency and stiffness in optical tweezers,” Optics Communications (2002)). The lower trapping efficiency of our system as compared to this range is likely influenced by factors such as focal diameter, as discussed above.

Furthermore, waveguide power handling is a limitation of the current system which has limited the maximum trap stiffnesses we have explored in this work. We plan to address this in future work by recreating the system in silicon nitride, another common waveguiding material with much better powerhandling properties than silicon. This is discussed in more detail in **Reviewer 2, Response 9** . The trap stiffness and drag rates scale with power, and so one simple way to increase these figures of merit is by increasing the input power to the waveguides. This is complicated by two-photon absorption in silicon waveguides, which limits their power handling. While we didn’t test the maximum power that could be input into our device, we noticed that spot brightness started to plateau around 50 mW, corresponding to a projected trap stiffness of around 0.012 pN/µm. This is not a significant improvement over what was demonstrated in the paper. In order to significantly raise the trap strength, future work could include reproducing the device in silicon nitride, which has a significantly higher power handling capability (this is a straightforward design to include on future chip hardware tapeouts at the foundry, and our group has produced multiple OPA devices to date in silicon nitride). This is discussed in the revised manuscript on Page 11:

“Second, silicon nitride could be used as the waveguiding material for the integrated OPA to improve the optical power handling capability of the waveguides and enable significantly more powerful optical tweezers that operates in a different force regime (standard silicon waveguides have limited power handling capability due to two-photon absorption [44]).”

In order to manipulate a 7x7 array of beads simultaneously, we would need to holographically encode such an array into our OPA system. We discuss how we would perform this in future work in **Reviewer 3, Response 3** . This system will likely be more lossy than our current device, as well as require sufficient power-per-trap, and so it is reasonable to expect that a laser in the range of a few watts would be needed. Cai et. al use a 5W laser in their work. While this is a different scale of manipulation and powers from what we consider in this work, it does seem possible as a potential application of OPA optical tweezers if so desired, and we have added a note to this effect on Page 11 of the revised manuscript: “These future OPA architectures could also be designed to encode advanced holographic emission patterns of interest [45], such as closely-spaced arrays of traps for high-throughput trapping applications [32,46].”
Applications

**Reviewer 2, Comment 5:** Although I do think there could be merit in a high through-put, photonic device for OT applications, I do not find the application to cell stretching convincing, and the general optical tweezing capability is not really competitive.

(i) Optical deformation of biological cells is a mature subject with a lengthy literature. The first report may be from Guck et al. in 2005 (Jochen Guck et al, "Optical Deformability as an Inherent Cell Marker for Testing Malignant Transformation and Metastatic Competence", Biophysical Journal (2005)). This article and other works by Guck et al. describe methods to understand optically induced cell deformation, extract elastic constants and use these measurements to diagonse pathologies. A review article describes much early work ("Optical tweezers for single cells", Journal of the Royal Society, Interface (2008)). A more recent review article compares measurements of cell mechanical properties acquired with various approaches, including optical stretching: "A comparison of methods to assess cell mechanical properties", Wu et al., Nature Methods (2018). This article shows how established this field has become. By comparison, I do not find the work on cell stretching, that appears in the article under review, to be particularly persuasive as an application. In particular, the mechanism whereby the cell is deformed is not described, and no attempt has been made to extract elastic properties.

**Reviewer 2, Response 5:** There is indeed a mature literature on optical cell deformation, with important applications in both basic science and applied technologies such as diagnostics. For this reason, we chose optical stretching of a cell as a highly relevant proof-of-concept experiment. We do not feel, however, that it is within the scope of this work (which is focused on demonstrating integrated tweezers hardware development) to lend new insight into the field of cell stretching or perform theoretical analyses of the

mechanisms behind the cell response to optical forces. Rather, we intended to demonstrate that our system can be used in cell experiments, enabling broader accessibility to research in optical cell deformation for those who do have the research background to make such advancements. This is emphasized on Page 10 of the revised manuscript:

“Herein, we report the first cell experiments with single-beam integrated optical tweezers, performing optical stretching on TIB-49 mouse lymphoblast cells as one example of a proof-of-concept experiment.”

**Reviewer 2, Comment 6:** (ii) More general optical tweezing. In addition to "cell stretching" the authors also describe trapping and tweezing of microspheres - itself useful in biophysics. Although it's clear that the objects are weakly trapped in the xy plane, it is not obvious that they have been trapped in the z direction. Typically, stiffnesses are weaker in this direction. Since the optical beams generated by the OPA are not tightly focused, the stiffnesses are weak compared to those found in conventional HOT, and it is possible that there is little or no confinement in the z direction.

**Reviewer 2, Response 6:** The reviewer brings up a valid point that, in this case, there is little confinement in the z-direction. For this particular application, all the polystyrene beads in a given sample came to rest near the surface of the coverslip and there wasn’t a need for strong confinement in the z-direction. To achieve a tighter focus along this dimension, an array with a larger aperture or smaller focal length can be used. In general, a larger aperture is preferred, as smaller focal lengths require a steeper phase gradient across the array dimension and, as a result, are more fabrication sensitive. Such a larger aperture can be achieved by adding additional antennas and increasing their length, which will add to the total footprint of the OPA. This is clarified on Pages 6-7 of the revised manuscript:

“As shown in Fig. 3(c), when the laser is off, the target sphere of interest exhibits significant displacement; in contrast, when the laser is on and the sphere is trapped, its motion is severely restricted, indicating that it has successfully been caught in a potential energy well created by the optical trap (note that the trap provides little confinement along the z axis).”
## Overall Significance

**Reviewer 2, Comment 7:** For the reasons described above, I do not think that the reported results warrant publication in Nat. Comms. That said, the device is neat and novel and certainly deserves publication somewhere more technical. Had the authors demonstrated high through-put measurement of the mechanical properties of cells - that could be a different matter but even then there is stiff competition, particularly in terms of the work of Jochen Guck over the preceding decades.

**Reviewer 2, Response 7:** We hope that in light of clarifications about the most significant parts of this work, as in **Reviewer 2, Response 1** and **Reviewer 3, Response 6** , we were better able to convey to the reviewer the impact of the system presented in this work and why it would be of particular interest to a broader scientific audience such as _Nature Communications_ , whose readership includes many of the researchers outside of the fields of optics and biophysics who could most benefit from the broader accessibility to optical tweezers that integrated photonic circuits can offer. This work uses a novel mechanism to realize an appreciable step forward in the active research area of integrated optical traps. These integrated systems have several advantages over their usually more feature-rich bulk-optic counterparts, as we have highlighted throughout our responses, especially for applications where the cost, size, and complexity of such systems present a major roadblock to their implementation.
## SUGGESTIONS FOR IMPROVEMENT

Although I think the work presented in the article is correct, valid and perfectly sound I do, as indicated above, feel that its significance is lacking. Below I make a few suggestions that could improve or strengthen the work.

**Reviewer 2, Comment 8:** (i) Focusing with an OPA. Clearly, the authors demonstrated focusing sufficient to trap particles, albeit a little bit loosely. It would be really interesting to know more about the limits of this approach. What are the limits on the dimensions of the focal spot? what influence does the discreteness of the antennas have?

**Reviewer 2, Response 8:** The limits on the minimum dimensions of the focal spot can be derived from the Rayleigh criterion, and will scale inversely with aperture size and linearly with focal height of OPA. In this way, the FWHM can be significantly reduced by either increasing aperture size or decreasing focal height (as shown in the figure below).

A discussion regarding these points has been added on Page 4 of the revised manuscript: “The dimensions of the resulting focal spot, which impact the trapping efficiency, scale inversely with the OPA aperture size and linearly with the OPA focal height [23], allowing the characteristics of the system to be adjusted to fit the desired application. In this demonstration, we target polystyrene beads and cells with sizes around 10 µm. As a result, an aperture size of 1 mm[2] and focal height of 5 mm were chosen to provide a reasonable tradeoff between trapping efficiency, focal height, and system footprint.”

The reviewer astutely raises the point that the antennas are discrete elements, which has the effect of introducing grating lobes to the emission pattern, as discussed in **Reviewer 1, Response 3** . However, since these lobes are at a relatively large angle, they are far out of both the field of view and focal plane of experimentation, and thus their main impact on the system is reducing efficiency by drawing power from the main radiation lobe (see figure below that shows the simulated emission pattern). Subwavelength grating spacing can be explored as part of future work, and is particularly interesting as part of systems which have more complex holographic patterns encoded into them, such as arrays of optical traps, where the additional element density will improve the fidelity of the emission profile. **Reviewer 2, Comment 9:** (ii) Optical trapping and tweezing. Given answers to (i), what are the limits on the trap stiffness, drag rates etc.

**Reviewer 2, Response 9:** The FWHM of the trap will certainly affect the trapping efficiency, and therefore adjusting focal height and aperture area as described in **Reviewer 2, Response 8** are one way of improving the trap efficiency. **Reviewer 2, Comment 10:** (iii) Scalability. One of the appeals of using integrated photonics is that it could be scalable - to multiple traps, performing multiple measurements. However, if independent control of each trap is not required, multiple traps can be connected through a central bus waveguide and served by a single laser source. For many independently controlled traps, one would want to move towards the electrically controlled steering described in **Reviewer 2, Response 2** . Limits on the dimensions of the focal spot are less relevant to the degree to which the system can be multiplexed, except for the point that focal spot diameter can be decreased by increasing aperture size, which would decrease the total number of traps that could be placed on a single die.

As far as the technical details of CMOS fabrication, the maturity and repeatability of these processes makes it rather simple to “copy-and-paste” single traps in order to create highly multiplexed systems, as well to mass-produce these systems at scale. ## **Response to Comments from Reviewer 3:**

In “Optical Tweezing of Microparticles and Cells Using Silicon-Photonics-Based Optical Phased Arrays”, Sneh et al. present integrated, single-beam optical tweezers generated with optical phased arrays (OPAs). With their device, the authors demonstrate trapping of polystyrene microspheres 5 mm above the surface of the chip, a standoff distance over two orders of magnitude larger than that previously demonstrated with integrated optical tweezers. They demonstrate a method for steering the trap over a mm range by varying the input laser wavelength. Finally, as a proof-of-principle demonstration of the capabilities of the OPA optical tweezers, they trap and deform a single mouse lymphoblast cell.

**Reviewer 3, Comment 1:** Overall, the manuscript details an interesting new approach for integrated optical tweezers. However, there are critical questions on the utility and compatibility of the device, and the claims

made in the text that the work is paradigm-shifting were not convincing overall. While the current device likely improves over previous designs, the case for the significance of these improvements was lacking. In its present state, the work appears more suitable for a specialized journal (e.g. one with a focus on photonic devices), and not of sufficiently broad interest to warrant publication in Nature Communications. The main criticisms of the manuscript and specific comments are enumerated below.

**Reviewer 3, Response 1:** Note that we have removed the claim of “new paradigm for integrated optical tweezers” from the manuscript on Pages 1, 3, and 12. Instead, we clarify that this is indeed a “new modality for integrated optical tweezers” as suggested by the reviewer. (Prior integrated optical tweezers were generally limited to the operating modality of evanescent fields, while we are introducing a new operating modality of using a focused beam generated using an integrated OPA which is a fundamentally different electromagnetic operating principle and allows for significantly larger standoff distances and arbitrary active tweezing functionality).

Detailed discussions regarding the reviewer’s questions about the significance of the improvements enabled by this work, the utility of the system, and the journal selection are included below in the remaining comments to the reviewer, specifically in **Reviewer 3, Response 2/3/4/5/6** .
## Main comments:

In the text, the authors claim that “integrated optical tweezers have the potential to enable highly compact, low cost, and high throughput optical manipulation when compared to standard bulk-optical tweezers” (lines 8-10) and “this OPA-based approach combines the advantages in cost, footprint, complexity, and throughput of integrated tweezers with the functionality of state-of-the-art bulk-optical systems” (lines 316318). It is not clear that these claims are substantiated in the manuscript. Specifically:

**Reviewer 3, Comment 2:** On the low cost claim, the OPA-based device requires a tunable-wavelength IR laser source for trap steering, which can be quite expensive (a quick search reveals that a used Agilent system like the one used here costs $30-40k). This cost alone approaches that of some bulk optical trap instruments.

**Reviewer 3, Response 2:** This point is addressed as well in **Reviewer 2, Response 2** . The OPA-based system is tested in this work with a relatively high-end laser in order to maximize reproducibility and explore the capabilities of the device, but it is important to differentiate between the system itself and the laser attached to it, which can be exchanged depending on the demands of the experiment at hand. We agree that this was insufficiently addressed in the original manuscript, and needs to be discussed in-depth in the text, particularly given the wider readership of _Nature Communications_ , in order to make clearer the impact of the system. This has been addressed through a number of edits in the manuscript, as described throughout this response.

Secondly, there is a growing body of literature on integrated laser systems, including tunable ones (see P. A. Morton et. al, “Integrated Coherent Tunable Laser (ICTL) With Ultra-Wideband Wavelength Tuning and Sub-100 Hz Lorentzian Linewidth,” APL Photonics (2022)). In the future, we could realize integrated optical tweezers in their entirety on chip, without the need for an external laser. A discussion on both of these points is now included in the revised manuscript on Page 9: “Although these experiments were performed with a benchtop tunable laser in order to accurately characterize the system and maximize

repeatability, this functionality and wavelength tuning range could be readily achieved by powering the system using an inexpensive laser diode with thermal tuning or even an on-chip integrated tunable laser on the same photonic chip [30,31].”

**Reviewer 3, Comment 3:** On the throughput claim, the current work does not demonstrate how the OPAbased device can be scaled to generate arrays of traps for high-throughput applications. Based on the mm footprint of the device (Fig. 1), it is unclear how multiple traps with reasonable lateral spacing (of a few μm) could be generated for such applications, and how each trap could be controlled individually, since the laser wavelength seems to be the only adjustable parameter.

**Reviewer 3, Response 3:** One of the key advantages of integrated optical phased arrays is that they enable the emission of arbitrary patterns of radiation, dependent on the phase encoding at each element. This flexibility enables in future work the ability to design a similar system that has an array of focal spots as opposed to one. As for controlling each trap individually, this is indeed a complex problem that would require the ability to actively tune many elements in parallel in order to realize independent control of each focal spot. If this design challenge can be met, the same algorithms that are fed in to spatial light modulators in holographic bulk optical tweezers can be used to program the optical phased arrays as well. Our group has already in prior work demonstrated encoding of such holographic information into an OPA in order to produce more complex emission programs, i.e., J. Notaros et. al. “Integrated-Phased-Array-Based VisibleLight Near-Eye Holographic Projector”, CLEO (2019). A discussion of holographic OPA-based optical tweezers has been added into the revised manuscript on Page 11: “These future OPA architectures could also be designed to encode advanced holographic emission patterns of interest [45], such as closely-spaced arrays of traps for high-throughput trapping applications [32,46].”

It’s important to note that lateral spacing on the millimeter scale is also very interesting for highthroughput applications. For example, diagnostic tools, where one trap operates over a single channel, with several channels multiplexed per chip, entail such spacing. For such an application, the OPA system we have designed can be simply “copy-and-pasted” many times over on the silicon chip – this is one of the advantages of silicon photonics as a whole. A note on this has been added to the revised manuscript on Page 11: “Fourth, by leveraging the small form factor and high integration density enabled by CMOS processing, multiple integrated OPA tweezers could be integrated together in a massively parallel configuration, enabling applications in high-throughput cell sorting and diagnostic tools.”

Moreover, in general, we did not intend to emphasize in particular the high-throughput nature of the device, as we don’t exploit it in this work, but rather mention it as one of the many advantages of moving to integrated systems. As a result, we have made several edits to de-emphasize this point and raise the importance of others, in order to make the intended key impacts of our work clearer to readers. These changes to the manuscript are also highlighted in **Reviewer 2, Response 3** .

On Page 3, the phrase high-throughput was removed from the following sentence: “Overall, this work introduces a new modality for integrated optical tweezers, significantly expanding the utility and compatibility of integrated tweezers with both common biological experiments and emerging _in-vivo_
trapping research by extending their focal heights to the millimeter scale, with promising applications ranging from DNA and protein experiments to cell manipulation and sorting.”
Increased trapping throughput as a potential application is now mentioned only very briefly throughout the manuscript.

**Reviewer 3, Comment 4:** On a related point, the authors claim that the OPA-based device achieves the functionality of state-of-the-art bulk optical tweezers, but this seems to be an overstatement. Most standard bulk optical tweezers setups nowadays can control the trap position in all 3 dimensions (2 lateral and 1 axial), and in setups with multiple traps (usually two), each trap can be controlled independently. This capability is essential for manipulating individual molecules or cells. There does not seem to be an obvious way to steer the trap in more than one dimension with the current device. Furthermore, standard bulk optical tweezers instruments detect the position of the trapped object by imaging the deflection of the trapping beam (or of a separate detection beam) by that object onto a position sensitive photodetector. This method provides much more sensitive and higher-bandwidth detection than bead tracking by video imaging used in this manuscript. It is not at all clear if the OPA-based device could be compatible with standard detection methods of bulk optical tweezers.

**Reviewer 3, Response 4:** The original intention of the sentence where this claim was made was to highlight that the much of the functionality that integrated optical tweezers have lacked to date, such as stand-off distance and trap steering, are provided in the system described in this paper. We agree with the reviewer that the statement as originally written does not read this way and have changed it to be more accurate and clarify that our system is by no means on par with the latest commercial bulk-optic systems (although it does bring integrated optical tweezers a significant step closer to the functionality enabled by these tools). The revised statement is on Page 12 of the manuscript:
“This OPA-based approach offers the advantages in cost, footprint, complexity, and mass producibility of integrated tweezers, while providing much of the functionality of bulk-optical systems.”

In response to the point about steering in more than one dimension, this can be achieved, as described in the future work section, by the addition of active steering. In the simplest form, where one dimension is wavelength and the second electrically steered by the addition of linear phase shifters across the array dimension, this implementation is relatively trivial. Ultimately, it is our goal to enable electrical trap steering in all three dimensions, a challenging design problem that will have significant implications for complex and tunable holographic emission from the field of integrated optical phased arrays in general. A note on this has been added to Page 11 of the revised manuscript: “Third, novel focusing OPA architectures that incorporate electro-optic or thermo-optic modulators could be developed that enable nonmechanical two- or three-dimensional steering of the focal spot and do not require a tunable laser source [23]. These future OPA architectures could also be designed to encode advanced holographic emission patterns of interest [45], such as closely-spaced arrays of traps for high-throughput trapping applications [32,46].” However, it is important to note that many experiments involving the manipulation of molecules or cells only require a single spot and one dimension of steering. Therefore, while we intend to pursue more degrees of freedom in movement in future work, we feel that the current steering only in the antenna dimension does not significantly affect the significance of the work as a significant advance in the capabilities of integrated optical tweezers.

Finally, position detection of the trapped object using the deflection of the trapped beam is certainly an interesting idea, as it eliminates the need for a separate camera and lens system. Since passive integrated photonic circuits are reciprocal devices, this is a valuable functionality that can be certainly be developed in a future iteration of the system, and we thank the reviewer for the suggestion. Indeed, this highlights one of the strengths of using integrated photonics to develop optical tweezers, as the necessary components for such an upgrade, including germanium photodetectors, have already been developed by our group and

others in the field and can be readily monolithically incorporated into the system even from standard fabrication process development kits offered by foundries such as AIM Photonics. A discussion of this has been added to Page 11 of the revised manuscript:

“Fifth, by taking advantage of the advanced functionality enabled by CMOS processing, OPA tweezers could be monolithically integrated with germanium detectors, a standard offering in existing siliconphotonics process design kits [19], to create optical tweezers that simultaneously measure the position of the trapped object using the deflection of the trapping beam.”

**Reviewer 3, Comment 5:** In contrast to what is claimed in the text (see also the table in Fig. 1), trap steering is also possible in microlens array systems by changing the input beam incidence angle. This is true of any system that uses a lens to focus the beam to generate optical traps. The beam steering capabilities of the current device thus does not appear to be unique among integrated tweezers.

**Reviewer 3, Response 5:** While trap steering is achievable by changing the input beam incidence angle in micro-lens arrays, these are not integrated optical systems, nor are any systems using a bulk lens for focusing. Our work, as an integrated system, provides many advantages, including cost and massproducibility, over the aforementioned types of bulk-optical tweezers. The advantages of using an integrated system, such as cost, form-factor, complexity of operation, and mass-producibility, are discussed as well in **Reviewer 2, Response 1** and are critical to the significance of the work. Silicon-photonics systems have been widely published in high-impact journals, and specifically implementations of integrated optical tweezers have been published throughout the years in Nature portfolio journals [11,13,14].

In the specific case of bulk optical tweezers, the cost, size, and complexity of operation of these tools have limited their broader accessibility, especially to biology labs which lack the infrastructure or expertise to operate complex optical research tools but often have insight into some of the most interesting questions that these tools can be used to answer. This is one of the central reasons we chose to submit to _Nature Communications_ as opposed to more technical optics journals, which are less likely to be read by researchers from such labs. The aforementioned points are mentioned in the manuscript on Page 1:

“However, since standard optical tweezers consist of benchtop systems comprised of bulk-optical components, their cost, complexity, and need for specialized laboratory equipment have limited broad access to these standard bulk-optical tweezers.”

“While these systems offer significant advantages in form factor and complexity compared to standard bulk-optical systems, they have been restricted to trapping either directly on or within several microns from the surface of the chip (Fig. 1(b)). This significantly limits their widespread applicability in biophysics and cell experimentation, which typically involve sterile glass coverslips or cell culture wells that are at least 150 µm thick, since their focal heights are too short to penetrate into these standard sample chambers. Without the ability to use these ubiquitous methods of sample preparation, these prior integrated optical tweezers could only be used in a narrow set of experiments, such as with back-end-of-the-line microfluidics fabricated on top of the chips, which require additional time to fabricate, often necessitate disposal of the chip after each experiment due to contamination, and are non-sterile surfaces that are not compatible with the majority of biophysics, and especially cell, research. As such, extending standoff distances to the millimeter scale to enable compatibility with these standard sample-preparation methods is an important requirement for integrated optical tweezers to become a practical technology (and could even enable demonstrations in emerging _in-vivo_ tweezing applications that require millimeter-scale standoff distances [7]).”

**Reviewer 3, Comment 6:** Several times in the text, the authors also make the claim that “integrated demonstrations to date have been fundamentally limited to micron-scale standoff distances”, but the advantages of mm-range standoff distances achieved with this OPA-based device are never adequately explained or justified. Most bulk optical tweezers operate a few microns from the sample chamber surface (particularly in systems using an oil immersion objective lens), and this distance is more than adequate for single-molecule measurements. For trapping mammalian cells, distances of order 10 μm are required, and this is achievable with some bulk optical tweezers setups (e.g. with a water immersion lens) and also with microlens arrays (see Fig. 1). It is unclear why the authors consider the large standoff distance to be a major breakthrough.

**Reviewer 3, Response 6:** This point is critical to understanding the significance of the work, and, in response to this comment, we will make an effort to both revise the manuscript to convey this point as clearly as possible, as well as to explain here within the reply.

First, it is important to clarify what is meant by standoff distance. As the reviewer notes, most experiments with optical tweezers operate in a focal plane a few microns over the surface of the sample chamber. Standoff distance as defined for integrated systems is not, however, relative to the sample chamber, but rather to the optical tweezer, for example the lens or the integrated photonic system. The very fact that these experiments use a sample chamber, which is usually a glass coverslip with thickness over 100µm, demonstrates that a standoff distance larger than the few microns offered by existing integrated optical tweezers is needed for this experiment (current integrated optical tweezers are fundamentally limited to trapping within a few microns from the surface of the chip). Since this point is crucial to the field and what we have proposed, we have highlighted more explicitly the need to address the issue of standoff distance on Page 2 of the revised manuscript with the following added longer explanation:
We have also added a note about this on Page 3:

“Overall, this work introduces a new modality for integrated optical tweezers, significantly expanding the utility and compatibility of integrated tweezers with both common biological experiments and emerging _invivo_ trapping research by extending their focal lengths to the millimeter scale”
This is also noted in the results section on Page 7 of the revised manuscript:

“This is the first demonstration of an integrated optical trap able to operate at a millimeter-scale standoff distance, allowing for interaction with samples in standard glass coverslips, eliminating the need for complex microfluidics packaging, and enabling compatibility with a greater variety of samples.”

A sentence has also been added on Page 10, which clarifies that cell experiments are difficult to perform on existing integrated optical tweezers, which trap only a few microns over the surface of the photonic chip and therefore can’t be used with the coverslips and other sample chambers that are ubiquitous in experiments with bulk-optical tweezers. The use of coverslips and the like is not just a matter of cost and convenience. They are sterile surfaces, often passivated or functionalized, and optimized for high image quality:

“Importantly, the inability to use prior integrated optical tweezers with sterile coverslips or cell culture wells due to their short focal heights, which are too short to penetrate into these sample chambers, has made such demonstrations difficult to realize until now.”

It’s also worth noting briefly why extending the focal length is highly non-trivial and therefore has remained until now an unsolved question. Most existing demonstrations of integrated optical tweezers rely on exponentially-decaying evanescent fields, which have a maximum very close to the surface of the waveguide and decay rapidly. The OPA-based optical tweezers operate using a fundamentally different, and novel, mechanism. In our system, the field is instead focused, similar to a bulk lens, within a focal plane of interest within the radiative near field of the array. This is explained in a few places, including on Page 2 of the revised manuscript:

“Specifically, [OPA-based tweezers] provide a promising approach to extending the standoff operating distance by orders of magnitude (resolving the fundamental limitation on operating distance imposed by using evanescent-field trapping modalities)…”

Other small edits have been added throughout the discussion section to convey this point more clearly as well. We hope that, through these edits and the explanation above, we have been able to more clearly and convincingly convey the significance of extending the standoff distance of integrated optical tweezers.
## Specific questions:

**Reviewer 3, Comment 7:** The authors show that they achieve high trap stiffnesses given the input laser power, with a stiffness of ~0.3 pN/nm per 10 mW power (see Fig. 3d). This is about one order of magnitude higher than for typical bulk optical traps at the same power. What accounts for the more efficient use of light in the OPA-based devices?

**Reviewer 3, Response 7:** Our impression from the literature, highlighted also by **Reviewer 2** , **Comment 4** is that ~3 pN/nm (0.003 pN/µm) at 10 mW power, as taken from the graph in Fig. 3d, is actually a relatively low trap stiffness as compared to bulk optical tweezers (this is not higher than typical). The reasons for this are discussed in greater detail in **Reviewer 2, Response 4** .

**Reviewer 3, Comment 8:** Does the trap stiffness change with position as the trap is steered? This is important to maintain a constant force as the trap is moved, for example in stretching a tethered molecule.

**Reviewer 3, Response 8:** This is an interesting question. The factors that would affect the trap strength as a function of position would be differences in shape or beam waist of the focus as well as its power. In our experience, both of these factors remain essentially constant, especially over the steering ranges used in this paper, as a few tens of microns in the focal plane translates to a very small change in angle of emission. In applications that utilize the full millimeter steering range of the device, however, we would expect to see a change in the spot diameter and, depending on the gain profile of the laser, variations in spot power, making these concerns more relevant. A note is added on trap stiffness consistency on Page 5 of the revised manuscript:

“Since steering within the tens of microns region of interest for typical trapping experiments requires only small changes in emission angle and, therefore, input wavelength, the emitted power and, consequently, trap stiffness remain relatively consistent as the trap position is steered (note that, if steering over the entire millimeter range is necessary, trap stiffness will begin to degrade).”

**Reviewer 3, Comment 9:** Could the authors estimate the maximum force generated in the traps? It seems they have the data to make such an estimate, based on their experiments steering the trap at different rates and observing when beads fall out (lines 229-234).

**Reviewer 3, Response 9:** The maximum force generated in the trap can be calculated from Stokes’ Law using the critical velocity at which a microsphere falls out of the trap. Using the fact that tweezing speeds were limited to around 150nm/s, a force of 0.028 pN can be calculated. This is good for an estimate, but it is not a particularly accurate way to perform this measurement. In order to measure the maximum trap force, a flow is usually applied counter to a stationary trap in order to determine critical velocity, in order to control for external variables and ensure that the bead will be in the potential maximum of the trap. In our experimental characterization setup, the position stages are manually controlled, and we would therefore not be able to induce a repeatable velocity on the bead in order to provide accurate measurements of maximum trapping force. For this reason, we decided not to include the metric of maximum trap force in the manuscript to ensure that we are not reporting a number that might not be completely accurate.

**Reviewer 3, Comment 10:** In Fig. 3b and 4b the authors should explain in more detail how they imaged the sample chamber. Why are the two bright dots on each side of the beads in the images? What kind of illumination was used? What kind of camera and video imaging rate was used? The authors could provide this information in the methods section on imaging (lines 362-365).
**Reviewer 3, Response 10:** Additional details addressing these points have been added in the methods section on Page 13:

“Microsphere movements were recorded using an iDS UEye 1480-LE-C-HQ visible camera, recording with 640x480 resolution at 13.5 FPS, using dual-arm fiber optic illumination. The recorded video was loaded into the ImageJ plugin TrackMate. Spots marking the microspheres’ position in a given frame were found with a Laplace of Gaussian detection algorithm using the reflections off the sides of the spheres, which present as two bright dots on the lateral edges of each bead.”

**Reviewer 3, Comment 11:** The cell stretching experiments (Fig. 5) were not clearly described. It seems that the cell must have been bound to the chamber surface for it to be stretched when steering the trap, otherwise it would just track with the trap. How was stretching achieved?

**Reviewer 3, Response 11:** The cell has some natural level of adhesion to the surface, sufficient that, under lower trap force, the edge of the cell in the trap is stretched while the opposite edge remains in place. This has been clarified in the revised manuscript on Page 10:

“The cell has some inherent attraction to the surface of the coverslip, and, as a result, the edge of the cell outside of the trap remains in its position and cell deformation as opposed to movement of the entire cell is observed.”
