That said, I would like to make the following points - which may inform the editors decision.

(1) The authors have emphasized the key importance of "mass manufacurability" . I agree that this is important, but I can think of papers (very good papers!) in which sophisticated, low cost, massmanufacturable optical devices are described. For example, "Robotic Microscopy For Everyone: The OpenFlexure Microscope", by JT Collins et. al., is a great paper with 100+ citations since it was published in 2020....in Biomedical Optics Express. Parenthetically, only small tweaks would be needed to convert this microscope into a versatile optical trap. Another example is the demonstration of a massmanufacturable optical trap published by De Coster et al in 2015 - this is published in Optics Express.
(2) I'm not so sure about Nat. Comms. but Nat. Methods explicitly states that characteristics like cheapness or mass-manufacturability of instruments are not reasons for publication.

So - in summary - I do think that the authors have improved the manuscript and responded appropriately to criticisms. The claims are supported by the text. My only misgiving is whether or not Nat. Comms. is the right place - and that decision I am happy to leave with the editor.

Finally - congratulations to the authors! I hope I do not come across as being hostile or combative. I like the work, and it will be interesting to see if it does move in the direction (e.g. mass production and availability) suggested in the article. In reality, I'm way too nice a person to do these reviews ;-) - but I am also aware that when one person gets their work into Nat. Comms., someone else does not....so one has to be completely honest...

**Reviewer 2, Response:** We thank the reviewer for the detailed comments and effort they have put into reviewing our work. Their suggestions have certainly strengthened our manuscript and were very helpful.

We feel that Collins et al. and De Coster et al., while excellent papers, are different from our paper in that they do not offer new modalities for robotics or fiber traps, respectively, but instead develop new implementations of existing methods. If, for example, Collins et al. were to develop their work into an optical trap, they would have replaced only the sample stage, lens housing, and perhaps the camera, while all the essential (and expensive) elements, such as a high-NA objective, that make an optical trap what it is would remain the same from a more expensive bulk-optics system.

In contrast, our work advances the field of integrated silicon-photonics-based tweezers by introducing focusing integrated optical phased arrays to perform optical trapping, an entirely new approach to integrated optical tweezers (we believe this demonstration is very novel and certainly first of its kind for our field of silicon photonics), and one that offers important advantages over existing work in the research area of integrated optical tweezers.

Moreover, while the editor would be best able to clarify this point (as the reviewer mentioned), we did not find any information indicating that cost or manufacturability are not reasons for publication in _Nature Communications_ . To the contrary, a quick search found many examples published in the journal over the past few years for which low cost or mass manufacturability were the primary merit [Liu et al., _Nature Communications_ , 2021; Sun et al., _Nature Communications_ , 2018; Takahashi et al., _Nature Communications_ , 2018]. Given that low cost is often a barrier to implementation, especially in interdisciplinary research, publishing such research both appears consistent with articles of interest to _Nature Communications_ and is of importance to its broad and international readership.
## **Response to Comments from Reviewer 3:**

In their revised manuscript “Optical Tweezing of Microparticles and Cells Using Silicon-Photonics-Based Optical Phased Arrays” and in their rebuttal, Sneh et al. have responded to the reviewer comments. In particular, they have clarified several points of confusion in the original text related to the improvements in standoff distance and to the optical trap performance (e.g. trap stiffness, confinement in the axial direction, maximum force).

**Reviewer 3, Comment 1:** While the manuscript is certainly improved by these clarifications, my overall assessment of the work and its suitability for Nature Communications has unfortunately not changed. In my opinion, while the integrated optical tweezers device described here has some useful design features that warrant publication, they are not of sufficient significance and impact for a general readership journal like Nature Communications. In their rebuttal, the authors have argued that “the cost, size, and complexity of operation of [bulk optical tweezers] have limited their broader accessibility, especially to biology labs” and that this is “one of the central reasons [they] chose to submit to Nature Communications as opposed to

more technical optics journals, which are less likely to be read by researchers from such labs.” Of course these statements are true, but I also believe this means that the instrument’s capabilities and performance must attain a sufficiently high standard to be of broad interest to the biology community. From this perspective, I believe the current method falls short on multiple fronts. Thus, my opinion is that the work is more suitable for a specialized journal.

**Reviewer 3, Response 1:** The use of silicon-photonics integrated optical phased arrays is a very novel approach for the field of integrated optical traps, and, as the first demonstration of this concept, it is to be expected that not all performance metrics will have had a chance to be optimized. We highlight this point to demonstrate that the parameters of the system as presented in this work can be further adjusted and improved in future work or by other groups in the field to greatly improve trapping powers or spot dimensions – indeed, we discuss at length in the manuscript several ways in which this can be achieved and expand on some of these points in Reviewer 3 Response 2 below. The utility of the device can also be appreciated by biology groups, even though this first demonstration may not yet provide the trapping stiffness they will need for all types of experiments, as low trapping force is by no means inherently a theoretical limitation of the OPA-based optical traps that we develop in the manuscript.

The real significance of this work is connected to the fact that it takes an approach to integrated optical trap design that is fundamentally different on a physical level from the previous evanescent-field integrated traps, which physically can not provide the millimeter-scale distances from waveguide to focal point that we develop in this work. This critically enables work with sterilized and functionalized coverslips or cell wells that are critical to many experiments (for example, in single-molecule DNA studies, the surface of integrated optical traps are not certified DNase/RNase free, and it will be extremely challenging, if at all possible, to functionalize them one way and then another for two different experiments). For the field of integrated optical devices, and particularly integrated optical traps, this work answers a major outstanding limitation of prior work, and we therefore believe represents an “important advance of significance to specialists within [the] field” [quote taken from the _Nature Communications_ Aims & Scope page] and will spur new ways of thinking about nanophotonic optical tweezers.
Main comments:

**Reviewer 3, Comment 2:** The device does not generate the trapping forces that biology labs would require for single-molecule studies and many cell stretching measurements. As clarified in the rebuttal, the maximum lateral trap stiffness attained here (see Figure 3: ~0.01 pN/um = 10-5 pN/nm at 40 mW) is several orders of magnitude lower than what is typical in bulk optical traps for similar input laser power. In addition, they estimate a maximum trapping force of 0.028 pN, which is at least three orders of magnitude lower than in a bulk optical trap. Importantly, as explained in Response #9 to Reviewer 2, scaling up the laser power does not seem to be a workable solution, as nonlinear effects appear to take hold. The authors estimate that the power plateaus around 50 mW, corresponding to a stiffness of 0.012 pN/um. (This also means that maximum trapping force would not increase appreciably beyond 0.03 pN). These low values are incompatible with many biophysical applications of interest.

In contrast, we note that the nanophotonic devices described in Ref. 11 (Ye et al. Nature Comm., 2022) a stiffness of 0.015 pN/nm and a force >20 pN could be attained, also 3 orders of magnitude higher than that reported here. In this case, Ye et al. are able to demonstrate single-molecule measurements stretching various DNA molecules and measurement protein-DNA interactions.

**Reviewer 3, Response 2:** The reviewer is correct in pointing out that, while the forces we generate here are sufficient to trap and manipulate objects of interest, the current work provides a lower trapping stiffness than bulk optical tweezers as well as some prior integrated optical trapping demonstrations. However, we hope to convince the reviewer that lower trapping stiffness is not a fundamental limitation to the integrated
optical phased array trap architecture, and can be increased significantly by using silicon-nitride waveguides or increasing the aperture size in future iterations of the device.

It is important to highlight that the powers listed in the paper are input powers from the laser. The actual power in the main beam is 14.5 dB lower than the power that comes out of the fiber coupled to the device’s input, with losses coming from edge couplers, splitter elements, waveguide loss, radiation to grating lobes, and other sources. Methods of reducing this loss are discussed in the manuscript, and include sub-wavelength spacing between grating elements and further optimization of constituent components. However, at the low 1-2mW powers that are actually emitted from the chip and used for trapping, the trapping stiffness is well in line with expectation. Ye et al., for example, uses “a low laser power input to the device (~150 mW)” [Ye et al., _Nature Comm.,_ 2022] to perform their experiments. This suggests that future iterations of this device will achieve much higher stiffnesses and maximum trapping forces.

While in silicon photonics it is common to present the laser power coming out of the fiber (as we did in the initial version of the manuscript) rather than the power emitted by the device, we understand that doing so will likely make our work harder to understand for readers from other fields, especially considering that optical powers are usually reported for optical power in the trap for bulk optical tweezers. We have therefore switched the wording in the manuscript to instead provide values for the optical power radiated from the chip into the optical trap (the optical power in the trap focal spot) to make it more clear for readers (especially those from the trapping community). This has been updated for clarity on Pages 5, 8, 9, and 11 in the revised manuscript, as well as in Fig. 3(d): “We measure an optical fiber to main lobe (i.e. trap focal spot) efficiency of approximately -14.5 dB”; “Figure 3(d) shows this measured trap stiffness as a function of optical power in the trap focal spot”; “an optical power of 1.58 mW in the trap focal spot”; “We positioned a cell in the optical trap with an optical power of 1.74 mW in the trap focal spot.”

This simplest and most straightforward way to increase the trapping stiffness in this device is to increase the input laser power. As the reviewer correctly notes, this is not possible in the current iteration of the device, as two-photon absorption limits the power handling of silicon waveguides. However, this is not an issue with silicon-nitride waveguides. For example, in Poulton et al., _Optics Express_ , 2016, a phased array was fabricated in silicon nitride with a power in the radiated main beam of 400 mW. Redesigning and fabricating the device presented in this work in silicon nitride would be a straightforward next step (our group already has a lot of experience in this for other demonstrations) that would enable high trapping stiffnesses and compatibility with an even broader range of biological experiments. For this reason, we hope to convince the reviewer that the reported trapping stiffness does not represent a limitation on the device architecture developed in this work, and that its significance can therefore still be appreciated by readers at the current trap forces demonstrated. This is discussed in the revised manuscript on Page 11:

“In the future, given the natural scalability and design flexibility of the CMOS-compatible fabrication platform used to produce these OPA tweezers, there are a number of natural opportunities to further evolve the system to both improve its performance and enable new functionality. First, the integrated OPA could be scaled to a larger aperture size [23] and the perturbation strength of the antennas in the OPA could be apodized [20-22], which would decrease the diameter and increase the symmetry of the focal spot [23], improvements which would further improve the trap stiffness and uniformity. Second, silicon nitride could be used as the waveguiding material for the integrated OPA to improve the optical power handling capability of the waveguides and enable significantly more powerful optical tweezers that operate in a different force regime (standard silicon waveguides have limited power handling capability due to twophoton absorption [46]).”

In addition to increasing laser power input to the device, by choice of aperture size and focal height, the focal spot size can be reduced further, increasing the gradient force exerted by the optical trap on its target. The limits on the minimum dimensions of the focal spot can be derived from the Rayleigh criterion, and will scale inversely with the aperture size and linearly with the focal height of the OPA. In this way, the spot size can be significantly reduced by either increasing aperture size or decreasing focal height. A discussion of this is included on Page 4 of the revised manuscript:

“The dimensions of the resulting focal spot, which impact the trapping efficiency, scale inversely with the OPA aperture size and linearly with the OPA focal height [23], allowing the characteristics of the

system to be adjusted to fit the desired application. In this demonstration, we target polystyrene beads and cells with sizes around 10 µm. As a result, an aperture size of 1 mm2 and focal height of 5 mm were chosen to provide a reasonable tradeoff between trapping efficiency, focal height, and system footprint.”

**Reviewer 3, Comment 3:** In their Response #6 to Reviewer 2, the authors also reveal that there is little confinement in the axial (z) direction. They write: “For this particular application, all the polystyrene beads in a given sample came to rest near the surface of the coverslip and there wasn’t a need for strong confinement in the z-direction.” This is an important point that should not have been omitted previously. If this statement is correct, then the bead is trapped only laterally and pushed against the surface of the coverslip, not as depicted in Fig. 4. In single-molecule measurements, the trapped bead should be suspended some distance above the coverslip; dragging a bead across it during a stretching cycle would lead to artifacts due to interactions with the surface. Again, this raises critical questions on the compatibility of the device with a host of biophysical applications.

**Reviewer 3, Response 3:** It is important to clarify that the bead or other objects of interest are not pushed against the upper surface of the coverslip by radiation pressure, but rather rest near the bottom surface of it during experimentation. We have experimentally determined that the beads are not in contact with either coverslip surface. When initially added to the coverslip, beads can be noticed to settle downwards into a given plane, and, when the sample dries out after the experiment is complete, they travel further downward and rest on the bottom surface of the coverslip. During the actual experiment, the bead remains stable in its vertical (z) position.

This configuration will likely be suitable for many experiments of interest, such as stretching and unzipping DNA [11]. However, when confinement in the z dimension is of experimental relevance, a different choice of parameters for the optical-phased-array aperture size and focal height can be chosen to provide tight focusing in this z dimension as well. In the figure below, we show graphs of the full width at half max (FWHM) of a beam in the vertical dimension (z) as a function of these variables. For example, a 1-mm aperture size and focal height of 1mm would provide a FWHM of 12.3 µm in the z dimension. Tight focusing in the vertical dimension, therefore, is not a fundamental challenge for the device developed in this work and could be experimentally demonstrated in future work. Clarification on this point has been added to Page 4 of the revised manuscript:

“Note that, for the aperture size and focal height chosen for this demonstration, the resulting focal spot size in the vertical dimension (z) is large, and the trap provides little confinement along the vertical axis. For many optical-trapping experiments, the lateral (x and y) trapping efficiency is usually more important than the vertical. However, some potential applications also require tight confinement in the vertical dimension. In these cases, a larger aperture size or shorter focal height could be chosen to provide micrometer-scale spot sizes in the vertical dimension, as well as the lateral dimensions.

## Specific comments:

**Reviewer 3, Comment 4:** In comment 8 from my referee comments, I asked if the trap stiffness change with position as the trap is steered. The authors responded that in their experience, this remained “essentially constant” over the steering range, but it was unclear if this was determined from measurements or if this was the authors’ expectation. Presumably the transmission efficiency of the device varies as a function of wavelength. This variation should be measured and reported.

**Reviewer 3, Response 4:** In our response to Comment 8 from the previous round of edits, when we said in our experience, we meant that we have taken experimental measurements and found that both power in the spot and size of the beam remain essentially constant over these small wavelength ranges. These experiments were performed by imaging the spot in the focal plane and measuring the brightness and FWHM of the spot over these wavelength ranges. More details on this experimental characterization of the focusing integrated optical phased array can be found in [23]. It is important to highlight that the wavelength range required to steer an object over tens of microns is only 1549-1551 nm; over this range, we have found through measurement that there is not a noticeable change in transmission efficiency. We have added the following statement on Page 5 of the revised manuscript to clarify this point:

“Since steering within the tens of microns region of interest for typical trapping experiments requires only small changes in emission angle and, therefore, input wavelength, the emitted power and, consequently, trap stiffness was experimentally found to remain consistent as the trap position is steered (note that, if steering over the entire millimeter range is necessary, the spot size will change [23] and, as a result, trap stiffness will begin to degrade).”

**Reviewer 3, Comment 5:** In Figure 3d, it seems that the trap stiffness vs laser power trend line does not extrapolate to the origin as it should. This is likely an artifact from measuring the variance in bead position over a finite time window (as the time increases, the variance will increase, leading to a lower estimate of the stiffness = kBT/<x^2>). This raises the question whether the authors are overestimating the trap stiffness. A more robust method to determine the trap stiffness is to measure the power spectral density in bead position (see for example Ye et al., Supplementary Figure 11).

**Reviewer 3, Response 5:** The reviewer raises a valid point that the graph of trap stiffness as a function of optical power should cross the origin, and correctly asserts that this is due to the use of a finite time window – if we were to record for a time approaching infinity, we would see the bead’s mean square displacement go towards infinity, and therefore trap stiffness would be zero. However, at intermediate to higher optical powers, as the bead is increasingly confined by the optical trap, the effects of the finite experimental time window on the mean squared displacement are expected to diminish, as discussed in [Perez-Garcia et al., _Biomed. Opt. Express_ 2023], [Sarshar et al., _J. Biomed. Opt._ 2014], and [Polin et al., _Opt. Express_ 2005].

This overestimation effect is most significant near zero optical power. At high optical powers, we confirmed that the trap stiffness generally converges rapidly as a function of capture time, and, therefore, the impact of the finite time window on the trap-stiffness estimation in Fig. 3(d) is less significant. At the lowest optical power of 0.07 mW, the trap stiffness did not fully converge, as anticipated due to the finite time window [Sarshar et al., _J. Biomed. Opt._ 2014]. This confirms (as the reviewer pointed out) that the finite time window does indeed affect the trap stiffness values reported, but it most significantly affects the values reported for the lower optical powers shown in Fig. 3(d).

While some studies perform a linear fit through the origin to their data [12], using this approach to fitting the data does indeed artificially increase the reported trapping efficiency, derived from the slope of this graph. In contrast, in our paper, we use a different approach to fitting the data to make sure we are not overestimating the fit. We do not forecast backward in our line of fit and do not anchor it through the origin, in order to express our data as directly and as accurately as possible to the reader (circumventing the accidental overestimation of the fit-line slope that could occur with this method).

We agree that it is useful to clarify this point for readers so they can understand why our graph does not pass through the origin, and we have now added clarification on this point, as well as new references to [Perez-Garcia et al., _Biomed. Opt. Express_ 2023] and [Sarshar et al., _J. Biomed. Opt._ 2014], to Page 8 of the revised manuscript: “Note that, at zero optical power, we expect the trap stiffness to reach zero and for our linear fit to therefore pass through the origin. The small nonzero trap stiffness at zero optical power that can be extrapolated from our trendline is an expected characteristic of trap stiffness measured using the equipartition theorem with a finite time window [30,31] (since zero stiffness corresponds to infinite positional variance for these measurements, an infinite time window is required to capture a stiffness of exactly zero; resultingly, any finite capture window will result in a nonzero reported stiffness, even for zero optical power). This overestimation effect is most significant near zero optical power [31]. In contrast, at higher optical powers, we observe that the trap stiffness generally converges rapidly as a function of capture time, and, therefore, the impact of the finite time window on the trap-stiffness estimation in Fig. 3(d) is less significant.”

Power spectral density is indeed an excellent method for determining trap stiffness, and is particularly useful in the presence of drift or noise, which will affect stiffness measurements based on mean squared displacement much more than power spectral density analysis [Horst and Forde, _Optics Express_ , 2010]. However, this method requires the use of a high-speed camera (Ye et al., for example, use a 1000fps camera to perform such measurements). This higher frame rate is necessary to characterize the corner frequency that is used to determine trap stiffness in a power spectral density plot, which is usually in the hundreds of hertz. The camera used in our study records at only 13.5 fps, and we do not have access to a high-speed camera with the appropriate frame rate for power spectral density analysis. For this reason, we have chosen, like many other works in the field, to determine trap stiffness using mean squared displacement, and hope the reviewer will agree that this offers a sufficient characterization of the stiffness and efficiency of the device we have developed in this work. We have added a note to the revised manuscript on Page 8 mentioning that a power-spectral-density technique could also be used to further improve the accuracy:
“In the future, with the use of a high-speed camera, power-spectral-density analysis could instead be used to more accurately characterize the trap stiffness at lower optical powers [11].”

## **Response to Comments from Reviewer 3:**

In their 2nd revision of the manuscript “Optical Tweezing of Microparticles and Cells Using SiliconPhotonics-Based Optical Phased Arrays” and in their rebuttal, Sneh et al. have responded to the latest reviewer comments. In particular, they have addressed two key criticisms that tempered my enthusiasm for the work. In their rebuttal, the authors have clarified that the laser power emitted from the chip is actually 30x lower than the input power, and that the stiffness could in principle be increased with silicon nitride waveguides or by increasing the aperture size of the device. One minor comment:

**Reviewer 3, Comment** : The authors clarify that the trapped beads “rest near the bottom surface [of the coverslip]” but “are not in contact with either coverslip surface”. Could the authors estimate the distance between the bead and coverslip surface? Is this consistent with the 5-mm standoff distance in their device design? It would be useful to the readers to know what an effective working distance could be in practice with a sample chamber such as the one used in this study.

**Reviewer 3, Response:** We thank the reviewer for the detailed comments and effort they have put into reviewing our work throughout the review process. Their suggestions have helped us to significantly strengthen this manuscript.

To clarify, the coverslip chambers that the samples were housed in have a thickness of 375 µm (this is mentioned on page 6 of the manuscript “creating a chamber with a thickness of 375 µm”). These coverslip chambers are then placed into the sample stage above the chip, approximately 5 mm above the surface of the chip (this is mentioned on page 6 of the manuscript: “The well containing the microsphere solution is then clamped into the sample stage above the chip.”). The height (and position) of the sample stage is adjusted such that the objects of interest lie at about the same height (and position) as the 5-mm focal plane of the beam emitted out of the OPA (this is mentioned on page 6 of the manuscript: “Using the positioning system on the sample stage, a target sphere is moved into the focal spot of the trap.”). Setting this height does not need to be a very precise adjustment, since the focal spot size in the vertical dimension is relatively large (as mentioned on page 4 of the manuscript “the resulting focal spot size in the vertical dimension ( _z_ ) is large”).

Since the detail explaining the microsphere position in the coverslip was not included previously in the manuscript (only in the reviewer response document), we added a new comment mentioning that the microspheres come to rest above the bottom surface of the coverslip chamber but not in contact with either coverslip to page 6 of the manuscript: “The microspheres come to rest slightly above, but not in contact with, the coverslip surface.”

## Optical tweezing of microparticles and cells using silicon-photonics-based optical phased arrays 

Received: 2 May 2023 Accepted: 29 August 2024 Check for updates 

Tal Sneh 1, Sabrina Corsetti 1, Milica Notaros1, Kruthika Kikkeri1, Joel Voldman[1] & Jelena Notaros 1 

Integrated optical tweezers have the potential to enable highly-compact, lowcost, mass-manufactured, and broadly-accessible optical manipulation when compared to standard bulk-optical tweezers. However, integrated demonstrations to date have been fundamentally limited to micron-scale standoff distances and, often, passive trapping functionality, making them incompatible with many existing applications and significantly limiting their utility, especially for biological studies. In this work, we demonstrate optical trapping and tweezing using an integrated OPA for the first time, increasing the standoff distance of integrated optical tweezers by over two orders of magnitude compared to prior demonstrations. First, we demonstrate trapping of polystyrene microspheres 5 mm above the surface of the chip and calibrate the trap force. Next, we show tweezing of polystyrene microspheres in one dimension by non-mechanically steering the trap by varying the input laser wavelength. Finally, we use the OPA tweezers to demonstrate, to the best of our knowledge, the first cell experiments using single-beam integrated optical tweezers, showing controlled deformation of mouse lymphoblast cells. This work introduces a new modality for integrated optical tweezers, significantly expanding their utility and compatibility with existing applications, especially for biological experiments.

Optical traps and tweezers enable trapping and manipulation of particles through non-contact forces caused by optical intensity gradients and photon momentum transfer[1] . Due to these properties, optical trapping has become a key technology for biological experimentation since it enables precise control over the position of and applied force on objects at the micron and submicron scale. For example, this technique has enabled insight into the biomechanics of DNA and motor proteins, helped classify and characterize cells, and yielded important data on the underlying biology of disease mechanisms[1][–][7] . However, since standard optical tweezers consist of benchtop systems comprised of bulk-optical components, their cost, complexity, and need for specialized laboratory equipment have limited broad access to these standard bulk-optical tweezers. 

Integrated-photonics-based optical tweezers offer exciting potential to resolve these challenges. Specifically, integratedphotonics-based tweezers can be mass manufactured in a compact form factor and at a much lower cost and can be densely integrated to increase trapping throughput. To date, integrated optical trapping has been demonstrated using evanescent fields from planar waveguides, optical resonators, and plasmonic devices[8][–][16] . While these systems offer significant advantages in form factor and complexity compared to standard bulk-optical systems, they have been restricted to trapping either directly on or within severalmicrons from the surface of the chip (Fig. 1b).

## Focusing integrated OPA system 

In general, an integrated optical phased array (OPA) is a system comprised of an array of antennas that are fed with controlled phase and amplitude inputs into each antenna to emit arbitraryradiation patterns off of the chip. If the antennas are fed with a uniform amplitude and a linear phase distribution, the array is limited to generating and nonmechanically steering a diffracting beam in the far field of the array (as has been shown in the majority of OPA demonstrations to date)[17][–][22] . An example simulated radiation pattern resulting from this traditional approach can be seen in Fig. 2a. In contrast, if a hyperbolic phase distribution, similar to the curvature of a lens, is applied across the antennas, the resulting radiation pattern will be tightly focused at a point in the radiative near field above the array (Fig. 2b)[23] .

This hyperbolic phase can be encoded modulo 2π, similar to a Fresnel lens, leading to the phase distribution shown in Fig. 2d. This novel focusing OPA modality and the resulting focused beamenablethe light intensity gradients required to perform optical trapping. 

To demonstrate this functionality, we designed and fabricated a splitter-tree-based focusing OPA system[23] . The system was fabricated in a CMOS-compatible foundry process at the State University of New York Polytechnic Institute’s (SUNY Poly) Albany NanoTech Complex on a 300-mm silicon-on-insulator wafer with a buried oxide thickness of 2 µm. The silicon device layer is 220-nm thick and was patterned with 193-nm immersion lithography. 

The system is designed to operate at a center wavelength of 1550 nm. At the system input, an inverse-taper edge coupler couples light into an on-chip silicon waveguide from an off-chip laser. A 9-stage splitter tree network comprised of compact Y-junction splitters[24] then evenly distributes the input power to 512 grating-based antennas with an antenna pitch of 2 µm. To apply the desired phase distribution for focusing in the array dimension (x), a phase bump device is placed before each antenna to impart a static phase delay dependent on the maximum width of the bump; the width of each bump is chosen such that the correct phase profile for focusing 5 mm above the chip is applied. Since the antennas are spaced with an antenna pitch larger than λ/2, the system also generates higher-order grating lobes in the array dimension; however, these lobes appear at larger angles and are far out of both the field of view and focal plane of experimentation, and, consequently, their main impact on the system is only reducing efficiency by drawing power from the main lobe.

The dimensions of the resulting focal spot, which impact the trapping efficiency, scale inversely with the OPA aperture size and linearly with the OPA focal height[23] , allowing the characteristics of the system to be adjusted to fit the desired application. In this demonstration, we target polystyrene beads and cells with sizes around 10 µm. As a result, an aperture size of 1 mm[2] and focal height of 5 mm were chosen to provide a reasonable tradeoff between trapping efficiency, focal height, and system footprint. 

Note that, for the aperture size and focal height chosen for this demonstration, the resulting focal spot size in the vertical dimension (z) is large, and the trap provides little confinement along the vertical axis.

For many optical-trapping experiments, the lateral (x and y) trapping efficiency is more important than the vertical. However, some potential applications also require tight confinement in the vertical dimension. In these cases, a larger aperture size or shorter focal height could be chosen to provide micrometer-scale spot sizes in the vertical dimension, as well as the lateral dimensions[23] . 

To characterize the fabricated system, we utilize an Agilent 81600B tunable benchtop laser source and an optical system to image the focal plane of the OPA onto an InGaAs infrared (IR) camera (see Methods for details). The resulting radiation pattern in the focal plane of the OPA is shown in Fig. 2e. The fabricated system focuses tightly at the designed focal height of 5 mm, with a power full-width half-maximum (FWHM) of approximately 6.4 µm along the array dimension (x) and 7.6 µm along the antenna dimension (y), closely matching the expected FWHM of 6.6 µm × 7.6 µm from simulation[23] . We measure an optical fiber to main lobe (i.e. trap focal spot) efficiency of approximately −14.5 dB, with primary sources of loss attributed to edgecoupling loss, waveguide propagation loss, Y-junction splitter losses, and antenna emission losses, including power radiated to the grating lobes. These experimental results confirm that this focusing OPA system satisfies the requirements for static optical trapping of polystyrene particles and cells. 

In order to enable the system to transform from a static optical trap to dynamic optical tweezers, the ability to precisely steer the position of the emitted focal spot is necessary.

To enable steering of the focal spot in one dimension using the OPA system, we vary the input wavelength, which changes the effective period of the radiating antennas and, as a result, their angle of emission[23] . As shown in Fig. 2f, the focal spot can be non-mechanically steered in the antenna dimension (i.e. in the y dimension) over a range larger than a millimeter 

—useful for positioning the spot relative to the target object when optical trapping, as well as finely steered with micron-scale accuracy for precision force and position sensing. Since steering within the tens of microns region of interest for typical trapping experiments requires only small changes in emission angle and, therefore, input wavelength, the emitted power and, consequently, trap stiffness was experimentally found to remain consistent as the trap position is steered (note that, if steering over the entire millimeter range is necessary, the spot size will change[23] and, as a result, trap stiffness will begin to degrade). Since the spot steering mechanism is fundamentally based on the Bragg condition, in theory, the only limitation on the fidelity of steering is the wavelength step size and the stability of the laser input. Common scientific benchtop lasers, such as the Agilent systems used in this work, offer wavelength step sizes and stabilities in the range of a few picometers, corresponding to theoretical spot position variation in the tens of nanometers; this is significantly smaller than the position variation of a trapped particle due to random motion for the trap powers under study.

Therefore, when used with most benchtop lasers, the strength of the trap and, as a result, the mean squared displacement of the trapped object will limit when two different trap locations will produce a meaningful displacement of the object. For applications where less precision is required, lower-cost laser diodes can also be used with the OPA optical tweezers; however, if temperature stabilization circuitry is not included with the laser, wavelength stability will begin to have a noticeable effect on the stiffness and maximum force of the trap. 

## Results 

Using this focusing integrated OPA system, we now demonstrate optical trapping and tweezing with an integrated OPA for the first time, increasing the standoff distance of integrated optical tweezers by over two orders of magnitude compared to prior demonstrations[9][–][15] . Specifically, we calibrate the trap force of the system and demonstrate both optical trapping and tweezing of polystyrene microspheres using the system. We then use the OPA system to perform, for the first time, cell experiments with single-beam integrated optical tweezers. Specifically, we show controlled deformation of mouse lymphoblast cells, a biologically-relevant technique that can be used to determine the elastic moduli of cells for both fundamental research and elucidation of disease mechanisms.

The setup used to characterize our integrated OPA-based optical trap is shown in Fig. 3a. The optical trap chip is mounted on a chuck, with a sample stage that supports either coverslips or small cell culture dishes mounted on a positioning system above the chip. Light is routed from a tunable benchtop laser source via an SMF-28e lensed fiber and is edge coupled to the system with 190 µW of power supplied at the input of the chip. The setup is visualized using either a 20X or a 100X Mitutoyo objective, and split into both visible and IR imaging paths using a dichroic mirror and relay lens.

To create a well for the solution of polystyrene microspheres, two coverslips are separated by double-sided tape, creating a chamber with a thickness of 375 µm, into which a 5.5% v/v solution of polystyrene microspheres suspended in deionized water is pipetted. Specifically, we use microspheres with a diameter of 10 µm and a 0.09-µm size distribution, as they have a similar size to human and mouse cells, such as lymphoblasts[26] . The microspheres come to rest slightly above, but not in contact with, the coverslip surface. The well containing the microsphere solution is then clamped into the sample stage above the chip. Using the positioning system on the sample stage, a target sphere is moved into the focal spot of the trap. Once the sphere moves stably into the center of the trap, its motion is recorded using a visible camera for 75 s. In contrast, at higher optical powers, we observe that the trap stiffness generally converges rapidly as a function of capture time, and, therefore, the impact of the finite time window on the trap-stiffness estimation in Fig. 3d is less significant. While stationary trapping is useful for many experiments, the ability to manipulate an object in a trap significantly extends the functionality and usability of optical traps. This functionality is known as optical tweezing, and is a capability absent in many integrated optical trapping demonstrations to date[12][,][13] . 

To enable this tweezing functionality, we leverage the nonmechanical spot steering capability of our OPA system to transform the system from a static optical trap to dynamic optical tweezers. As discussed above, we can vary the wavelength of the laser input into the focusing OPA system to non-mechanically steer the location of the spot emitted out of the OPA—i.e. set the trap position—with micron precision over a range of over a millimeter along the antenna dimension (Fig. 2f). The focal spot remains largely in the sample plane over a steering range of tens of microns.

Using this wavelength-control scheme and an optical power of 1.58 mW in the trap focal spot, we varied the trap position in the antenna dimension, with the polystyrene microsphere following its motion. To confirm that the microsphere was moving successfully due to repositioning of the focal spot and not due to any residual fluid velocity in the sample chamber, we non-mechanically steered the trap back and forth several times and observed the resulting position of the microsphere (Fig. 4b), confirming successful tweezing. Next, we showed repeated tweezing of the microsphere in a sine-wave pattern with two different frequencies, to demonstrate that the microsphere of interest can be steered in arbitrary patterns in one dimension. Specifically, we varied the input laser wavelength as a function of time using two sinusoidal patterns with wavelength ranges of ± 1 nm, at rates of both 0.059 and 0.048 cycles/min. The resulting position of the trapped microsphere was recorded and processed using TrackMate. The microsphere position (solid line) closely followed the focal spot position (dashed line) for both patterns, demonstrating manipulation with submicron precision over a range of tens of microns (Fig. 4c). 

To further confirm the functionality of the system, we then used our integrated optical tweezers to demonstrate tweezing at four different speeds. Specifically, we varied the input wavelength linearly as a function of time for four different wavelength sweep settings (5 pm/s, 6.25 pm/s, 8.33 pm/s, and 12.5 pm/s), resulting in focal spot travel speeds of approximately 60 nm/s, 75 nm/s, 100 nm/s, and 150 nm/s, respectively.

Figure 4d shows the resulting measured positions of the trap focal spot and of the target microsphere as a function of time as dashed and solid lines, respectively, for each of the four sweep settings. The microsphere is able to successfully follow the motion of the 

focal spot up to a wavelength sweep setting of around 12.5 pm/s (corresponding to a focal spot speed of approximately 150 nm/s), at which point the microsphere begins to fall out of the trap. At this point, the drag force on the particle through the water overcomes the force exerted by the trap, and the sphere lags behind the trap maximum until it falls out of the trap. Note that slightly higher manipulation speeds were attainable in the upwards direction than in the downwards direction, which can be attributed to the asymmetry in the focal spot pattern (Fig. 2e); this asymmetry is common to antennas with constant perturbations and can be improved upon by varying the perturbation strength along the length of the antenna[20][–][22] . 

Although these experiments were performed with a benchtop tunable laser in order to accurately characterize the system and maximize repeatability, this functionality and wavelength tuning range could be readily achieved by powering the system using an inexpensive laser diode with thermal tuning or even an on-chip integrated tunable laser on the same photonic chip[32][,][33] .

In addition, cells are easily contaminated, and their placement on unique substrates, such as silicon-photonics chips, can stress them and affect the behavior under study[40][,][41] . ## Discussion 

In summary, this work presents optical trapping and tweezing using an integrated OPA for the first time, increasing the standoff distance of integrated optical tweezers by over two orders of magnitude larger than prior demonstrations, significantly expanding their utility. We use a focusing integrated OPA to emit a tightly focused beam out of the chip and demonstrate successful trapping of polystyrene microspheres 5 mm above the surface of the chip, with the sphere’s motion significantly reduced due to the force of the trap. We next calibrate this 

optical trap system using the equipartition method, a common calibration method for bulk optical tweezers[28] , demonstrating consistent trap stiffness that scales linearly with power. We then nonmechanically steer the focal spot by varying the input laser wavelength to transform the system from a static optical trap to dynamic optical tweezers and demonstrate tweezing of polystyrene microspheres in one-dimensional patterns with high fidelity and submicron precision. Finally, we use these OPA tweezers to show controlled deformation of mouse lymphoblast cells (a biologically-relevant technique that can be used to analyze mechanical properties of cells for both fundamental research and applied studies to investigate disease mechanisms[42][–][45] ), a promising proof-of-concept demonstration that represents, to the best of our knowledge, the first cell experiments using single-beam integrated optical tweezers. 

In the future, given the natural scalability and design flexibility of the CMOS-compatible fabrication platform used to produce these OPA tweezers, there are a number of natural opportunities to further evolve the system to both improve its performance and enable new functionality.

First, the integrated OPA could be scaled to a larger aperture size[23] and the perturbation strength of the antennas in the OPA could be apodized[20][–][22] , which would decrease the diameter and increase the symmetry of the focal spot[23] , improvements which would further improve the trap stiffness and uniformity. Second, silicon nitride could be used as the waveguiding material for the integrated OPA to improve the optical power handling capability of the waveguides and enable significantly more powerful optical tweezers that operate in a different force regime (standard silicon waveguides have limited power handling capability due to two-photon absorption[46] ). Third, novel focusing OPA architectures that incorporate electro-optic or thermo-optic modulators could be developed that enable non-mechanical two- or three-dimensional steering of the focal spot and do not require a tunable laser source[23] . These future OPA architectures could also be designed to encode advanced holographic emission patterns of interest[47] , such as closely-spaced arrays of traps for high-throughput trapping applications[34][,][48] . Fourth, by leveraging the small form factor and high integration density enabled by CMOS processing, multiple integrated OPA tweezers could be integrated together in a massively parallel configuration, enabling applications in high-throughput cell sorting and diagnostic tools. Fifth, by taking advantage of the advanced functionality enabled by CMOS processing, OPA tweezers could be monolithically integrated with germanium detectors, a standard offering in existing silicon-photonics process design kits[19] , to create optical tweezers that simultaneously measure the position of the trapped object using the deflection of the trapping beam.

The large focal heights enabled by this approach allow for manipulation of samples in simple coverslips and sample chambers standard to biological experiments (and even the potential to probe into the body for future in-vivo applications[7] ), eliminating the need for complex microfluidics packaging that has been a necessary component of prior integrated optical tweezers demonstrations. This OPA-based approach offers the advantages in cost, footprint, complexity, and mass producibility of integrated tweezers, while providing much of the functionality of bulkoptical systems.

It thus represents a significant improvement in the future utility and compatibility of integrated optical tweezers for biological research and has the potential to open the door to a wide variety of experiments that have not been previously possible with prior implementations of integrated tweezers, spanning biophysics research with microsphere-conjugated molecules, single-cell experimentation and sorting, and emerging in-vivo trapping research. 

## Methods 

## Integrated-optical-phased-array chip fabrication 

The integrated-optical-phased-array system was fabricated in a CMOScompatible 300-mm-diameter wafer-scale silicon-photonics process at the State University of New York Polytechnic Institute’s (SUNY Poly) Albany NanoTech Complex. The process utilizes 300-mm-diameter silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafers with a 2-µm-thick buried oxide and a standard 220-nm-thick silicon waveguiding layer patterned using 193nm immersion lithography. Details are provided in[23] . 

## Experimental characterization setup 

The integrated OPA-based optical tweezers were characterized using an optical imaging system consisting of a microscope objective (Mitutoyo, either 20X/0.4NA or 100X/0.5NA), and separate IR and visible imaging paths. The microscope objective is connected to a dichroic mirror, which routes light into a visible camera and, via a relay lens, to an IR camera. This system is mounted on an optical breadboard with three axes of movement. The tweezers chip is mounted on a chuck. Light is routed from an Agilent 81600B tunable benchtop laser source through an Amonics erbium-doped fiber amplifier (AEDFA-C_20I-B) to an SMF-28e lensed fiber that is edge coupled to the silicon-photonics chip.

A sample stage that supports both coverslips and small cell culture dishes is mounted on a NanoMax positioning system above the chip. 

## Focal-spot and beam-steering characterization 

Characterization of the focusing beam formation and beam-steering functionality of the integrated optical tweezers was achieved by recording images of the light emitted out of the chip using a highresolution IR camera (SUI Goodrich SU640KTS-1.7RT). The height of the optical imaging system was then set such that images were taken at the focal plane of the OPA, with the focal plane location determined by scanning the system to the height above the chip where the focusing beam generates the minimum focal spot size. Focal plane images were then recorded over a range of input wavelengths to characterize the wavelength-induced non-mechanical beam-steering functionality. The locations of the intensity maxima were determined in MATLAB, and the resulting spatial offset of the beam in the steering direction was plotted as a function of the input wavelength. More details are provided in[23] . 

## Glass coverslip chamber assembly 

Chamberseither 300 µm or 375 µm in height wereformed between two #1 coverslips (VWR Microscope Cover Glasses, 16004-308) separated 

by several pieces of double-sided tape of thickness 75 µm according to the target chamber height. The chamber was mounted on a larger #1 coverslip for compatibility with the sample stage. 

## Polystyrene microsphere preparation 

Polystyrene microspheres (Duke Standards 4210A, 0.9% CV) were suspended in deionized water as a 5.5% v/v solution.

## Data acquisition and processing for microsphere experiments 

Microsphere movements were recorded using an iDS UEye 1480LE-C-HQ visible camera, recording with 640 × 480 resolution at 13.5 FPS, using dual-arm fiber optic illumination. The recorded video was loaded into the ImageJ plugin TrackMate. Spots marking the microspheres’ position in a given frame were found with a Laplace of Gaussian detection algorithm using the reflections off the sides of the spheres, which present as two bright dots on the lateral edges of each bead. Tracks were exported and processed in Python. 

## Cell culture 

TIB-49 mammalian cells were acquired from ATCC. Cells were maintained in a T-25 flask (ThermoFisher Scientific) containing RPMI-1640 Medium (ThermoFisher Scientific) with 10% Fetal Bovine Serum (ThermoFisher Scientific) and 1% 10,000 U/mL Penicillin-Streptomycin (ThermoFisher Scientific). Cells were stored at 37 °C in a humidified 5% CO2 incubator and were passaged one day prior to experimentation. Following harvesting, cells were washed through the use of a centrifuge and resuspended into a fresh media solution. 

## Cell tweezing and processing 

Cells were removed from the incubator and pipetted into a chamber with a thickness of 300 µm formed between two #1 coverslips. Cells were maneuvered into the focal spot emitted out of the integrated optical tweezers, which were then non-mechanically steered beyond the cell boundary. Cell deformation was recorded using a visible camera. The optical tweezers were then turned off to record the cell’s behavior in the absence of the force of the optical trap.

In this manuscript, the authors report the use of an OPA to demonstrate optical tweezing and trapping and show that the standoff distance is increased significantly. The manuscript is wellwritten and would be of interest to other scientists and engineers and I recommend publication in Nature Communications. I think it would make the paper stronger if my comments and questions below are addressed.
- Since grating based antennas are used, it would be useful for the authors to discuss the level of laser wavelength stability needed for the intended application.
- What phase adjustment resolution is needed for precise tweezer control?

- The authors should discuss the OPA calibration (and focal point distortion correction). What is the effect of the pitch of the elements being larger than wavelength (on the focusing the light into the focal point)?
- In Fig. 3(b), it would be useful to see if the motion of the microspheres that are not within the trap follows the expected Brownian motion model (within the monitored 75 second).
- What is the effect of the laser stability on the maximum speed of the tweezer movement (before the microspheres fall out of the trap)?
## **Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):**
Review of "Optical Tweezing of Microparticles and Cells Using Silicaon-Photonics-Based Optical Phased Arrays" by Sneh et al.

In this article the reviewers demonstrate a neat application of an optical phased array (OPA) incorporated into a silicon based photonic chip. By imposing a hyperbolic phase variation across the attennas comprising the OPA, a focus can be formed, in the array dimension, above the chip (5 mm above). Tuning the period of the grating-based antennas provides focusing in the orthogonal direction, apparently forming an optical trap. Varying the input wavelength modifies the Bragg condition allowing the focal spot to be shifted along the array dimension. The authors provide demonstrations of optical trapping and tweezing of dielectric microspheres and successfully manipulate a biological cell which deforms as it is dragged by the trap.

To start with, I should point out that I am primarily a theoretical physicist - with a strong interest in optical forces, structured light and photonics (including integrated photonics) in general, as well as stochastic thermodynamics and biophysics. Thus my experience is, perhaps, only tangentially relevant to this paper. However, I collaborate pretty continuously with experimentalists working in these fields and have done so for many years and so I think I have a reasonably broad overview of the relevant science.

My overall impression of this article is that it is not suitable for a high IF journal like Nat. Comms. but is, without doubt, suitable for a more technical journal, particularly one with a focus on instrumentation. The reason for this assessment is connected with the significance of the work, as described below, not the legitimacy or validity of the results. Indeed, I think this is a valuable contribution to the literature and may (possibly) have useful applications - the authors should be congratulated for this. Below I summarize my assemement of the significance of the work, make some minor scientific criticisms and suggest potential ways of strengthening the work.
## SIGNIFICANCE

The significance of this work derives from the significance of the instrument the authors have developed and on the useful applications that it enables especially those that have been demonstrated in the article. My judgement is the work falls short in both categories.

To start with the instrument. First, I agree that this is a neat and novel application of an integrated OPA. However, as I'm sure the authors would conceded, it does not do anything which cannot be done more precisely and flexibably with bulk optics, for example, by using a digital micromirror device, or similar. The virtues of this instrument lie, therefore, not on the uniqueness of its fundamental capabilities but on its cost, or on high-throuput applications. However,
(i) this approach uses a tunable laser to steer the beams in 1 dimension - and tunable lasers with the required specs. are not cheap, and,

(ii) the authors have not demonstrated the scalability of the approach either in its own terms or in comparison to conventional holographic optical traps (HOTs)- in contrast, it is routine to independently control multiple traps with holography. One very recent article ("Rapid tilted-plane Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm for holographic optical tweezers", Yanan Cai et al, Optics Express (2020)) demonstrated simultaneous trapping and manipulation of a 7 by 7 array of beads - I have seen still greater feats of parallel manipulation myself. The point is - if the authors wish to claim that their device is capable of very high throughput studies or assays, then I think this needs to be demonstrated to some degree. It should, for instance, be relatively trivial to outperform existing techniques in this respect. A demonstration of the simultaneous manipulation of 100s of particles, say, would be impressive. Finally,

(iii) the focal point generated by the OPA in this article is very weak compared with conventional optical trapping, for which beams are close to diffraction limited (i.e. beam waist radius comparable to half the wavelength). Although this may help when it comes to trapping the larger spheres and cells considered in this paper, the reported stiffnesses and drag rates remain low compared with those connected with HOT (e.g. this article reports stiffnesses of ~0.005 pN/micron - while stiffnesses of microspheres are often 10's of pN/micron). Connected with this, the reported drag rates are relatively low (e.g. Fig. 4 shows drag rates of ~10 microns in 100 seconds). These low stiffnesses and drag rates add to my questions about the scalability of this instrument. How much laser power would the authors expect to be required for manipulating, for example, the 49 spheres manipulated in the article by Cia et al, referred to above?
## Applications

Although I do think there could be merit in a high through-put, photonic device for OT applications, I do not find the application to cell stretching convincing, and the general optical tweezing capability is not really competitive.
(i) Optical deformation of biological cells is a mature subject with a lengthy literature. The first

report may be from Guck et al. in 2005 (Jochen Guck et al, "Optical Deformability as an Inherent Cell Marker for Testing Malignant Transformation and Metastatic Competence", Biophysical Journal (2005)). This article and other works by Guck et al. describe methods to understand optically induced cell deformation, extract elastic constants and use these measurements to diagonse pathologies. A review article describes much early work ("Optical tweezers for single cells", Journal of the Royal Society, Interface (2008)). A more recent review article compares measurements of cell mechanical properties acquired with various approaches, including optical stretching: "A comparison of methods to assess cell mechanical properties", Wu et al., Nature Methods (2018). This article shows how established this field has become. By comparison, I do not find the work on cell stretching, that appears in the article under review, to be particularly persuasive as an application. In particular, the mechanism whereby the cell is deformed is not described, and no attempt has been made to extract elastic properties.

(ii) More general optical tweezing. In addition to "cell stretching" the authors also describe trapping and tweezing of microspheres - itself useful in biophysics. Although it's clear that the objects are weakly trapped in the xy plane, it is not obvious that they have been trapped in the z direction. Typically, stiffnesses are weaker in this direction. Since the optical beams generated by the OPA are not tightly focused, the stiffnesses are weak compared to those found in conventional HOT, and it is possible that there is little or no confinement in the z direction.
## Overall Significance

For the reasons described above, I do not think that the reported results warrant publication in Nat. Comms. That said, the device is neat and novel and certainly deserves publication somewhere more technical. Had the authors demonstrated high through-put measurement of the mechanical properties of cells - that could be a different matter but even then there is stiff competition, particularly in terms of the work of Jochen Guck over the preceding decades.
## SUGGESTIONS FOR IMPROVEMENT

Although I think the work presented in the article is correct, valid and perfectly sound I do, as indicated above, feel that its significance is lacking. Below I make a few suggestions that could improve or strengthen the work.

(i) Focusing with an OPA. Clearly, the authors demonstrated focusing sufficient to trap particles, albeit a little bit loosely. It would be really interesting to know more about the limits of this approach. What are the limits on the dimensions of the focal spot? what influence does the discreteness of the antennas have?
(ii) Optical trapping and tweezing. Given answers to (i), what are the limits on the trap stiffness, drag rates etc.

(iii) Scalability. One of the appeals of using integrated photonics is that it could be scalable - to multiple traps, performing multiple measurements. If the approach really is scalable, this should be demonstrated to some degree, preferably to show that it really is competitive with existing techniques (HOT, DMD etc) with all the other advantages that come with them. How is scalability influenced by (a) the use of a tunable laser, (b) the limits on the dimensions of the focal spot and therefore on the gradient force, (c) technical considerations connected with chip manufacture.

(iv) Application to cell stretching. If the authors want to use this as a selling point, I really think more work needs to be done, to make this application look credible next to existing work. And this work needs properly referencing, especially the work of Guck, since the early work in 2005. First, the mechanism needs to be described. Assuming it is a true mechanical deformation, and not a deformation induced by nutrient flows for example, it should be easy to adapt an existing model for cell stretching to quantify the elastic properties. In particular, this system looks as if the streching is caused by a balance between drag induced fluid stresses, optical stresses and elastic stresses. The first two of these can be approximated analytically, allowing for the extraction of the third. In fact, you can probably get answers from COMSOL or equivalent.
## **Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):**

In “Optical Tweezing of Microparticles and Cells Using Silicon-Photonics-Based Optical Phased Arrays”, Sneh et al. present integrated, single-beam optical tweezers generated with optical phased arrays (OPAs). With their device, the authors demonstrate trapping of polystyrene microspheres 5 mm above the surface of the chip, a standoff distance over two orders of magnitude larger than that previously demonstrated with integrated optical tweezers. They demonstrate a method for steering the trap over a mm range by varying the input laser wavelength. Finally, as a proof-of-principle demonstration of the capabilities of the OPA optical tweezers, they trap and deform a single mouse lymphoblast cell.

Overall, the manuscript details an interesting new approach for integrated optical tweezers. However, there are critical questions on the utility and compatibility of the device, and the claims made in the text that the work is paradigm-shifting were not convincing overall. While the current device likely improves over previous designs, the case for the significance of these improvements was lacking. In its present state, the work appears more suitable for a specialized journal (e.g. one with a focus on photonic devices), and not of sufficiently broad interest to warrant publication in Nature Communications. The main criticisms of the manuscript and specific comments are enumerated below.
## Main comments:

In the text, the authors claim that “integrated optical tweezers have the potential to enable highly compact, low cost, and high throughput optical manipulation when compared to standard bulkoptical tweezers” (lines 8-10) and “this OPA-based approach combines the advantages in cost, footprint, complexity, and throughput of integrated tweezers with the functionality of state-of-theart bulk-optical systems” (lines 316-318). It is not clear that these claims are substantiated in the manuscript. Specifically:

On the low cost claim, the OPA-based device requires a tunable-wavelength IR laser source for trap steering, which can be quite expensive (a quick search reveals that a used Agilent system like the one used here costs $30-40k). This cost alone approaches that of some bulk optical trap instruments.
On the throughput claim, the current work does not demonstrate how the OPA-based device can be

scaled to generate arrays of traps for high-throughput applications. Based on the mm footprint of the device (Fig. 1), it is unclear how multiple traps with reasonable lateral spacing (of a few μm) could be generated for such applications, and how each trap could be controlled individually, since the laser wavelength seems to be the only adjustable parameter.

On a related point, the authors claim that the OPA-based device achieves the functionality of stateof-the-art bulk optical tweezers, but this seems to be an overstatement. Most standard bulk optical tweezers setups nowadays can control the trap position in all 3 dimensions (2 lateral and 1 axial), and in setups with multiple traps (usually two), each trap can be controlled independently. This capability is essential for manipulating individual molecules or cells. There does not seem to be an obvious way to steer the trap in more than one dimension with the current device. Furthermore, standard bulk optical tweezers instruments detect the position of the trapped object by imaging the deflection of the trapping beam (or of a separate detection beam) by that object onto a position sensitive photodetector. This method provides much more sensitive and higher-bandwidth detection than bead tracking by video imaging used in this manuscript. It is not at all clear if the OPA-based device could be compatible with standard detection methods of bulk optical tweezers.

In contrast to what is claimed in the text (see also the table in Fig. 1), trap steering is also possible in microlens array systems by changing the input beam incidence angle. This is true of any system that uses a lens to focus the beam to generate optical traps. The beam steering capabilities of the current device thus does not appear to be unique among integrated tweezers.

Several times in the text, the authors also make the claim that “integrated demonstrations to date have been fundamentally limited to micron-scale standoff distances”, but the advantages of mmrange standoff distances achieved with this OPA-based device are never adequately explained or justified. Most bulk optical tweezers operate a few microns from the sample chamber surface (particularly in systems using an oil immersion objective lens), and this distance is more than adequate for single-molecule measurements. For trapping mammalian cells, distances of order 10 μm are required, and this is achievable with some bulk optical tweezers setups (e.g. with a water immersion lens) and also with microlens arrays (see Fig. 1). It is unclear why the authors consider the large standoff distance to be a major breakthrough.
## Specific questions:

The authors show that they achieve high trap stiffnesses given the input laser power, with a stiffness of ~0.3 pN/nm per 10 mW power (see Fig. 3d). This is about one order of magnitude higher than for typical bulk optical traps at the same power. What accounts for the more efficient use of light in the OPA-based devices?
Does the trap stiffness change with position as the trap is steered? This is important to maintain a constant force as the trap is moved, for example in stretching a tethered molecule.

Could the authors estimate the maximum force generated in the traps? It seems they have the data to make such an estimate, based on their experiments steering the trap at different rates and observing when beads fall out (lines 229-234).
In Fig. 3b and 4b the authors should explain in more detail how they imaged the sample chamber. Why are the two bright dots on each side of the beads in the images? What kind of illumination was
used? What kind of camera and video imaging rate was used? The authors could provide this information in the methods section on imaging (lines 362-365).

The cell stretching experiments (Fig. 5) were not clearly described. It seems that the cell must have been bound to the chamber surface for it to be stretched when steering the trap, otherwise it would just track with the trap. How was stretching achieved?
Specific comments:

Lines 89-99: A reference is needed for the following statement: “the array is limited to generating and non-mechanically steering a diffracting beam in the far field of the array (as has been shown in the majority of OPA demonstrations to date).”

## **Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):**

In their revised manuscript “Optical Tweezing of Microparticles and Cells Using Silicon-PhotonicsBased Optical Phased Arrays” and in their rebuttal, Sneh et al. have responded to the reviewer comments. In particular, they have clarified several points of confusion in the original text related to the improvements in standoff distance and to the optical trap performance (e.g. trap stiffness, confinement in the axial direction, maximum force).

While the manuscript is certainly improved by these clarifications, my overall assessment of the work and its suitability for Nature Communications has unfortunately not changed. In my opinion, while the integrated optical tweezers device described here has some useful design features that warrant publication, they are not of sufficient significance and impact for a general readership journal like Nature Communications. In their rebuttal, the authors have argued that “the cost, size, and complexity of operation of [bulk optical tweezers] have limited their broader accessibility, especially to biology labs” and that this is “one of the central reasons [they] chose to submit to Nature Communications as opposed to more technical optics journals, which are less likely to be read by researchers from such labs.” Of course these statements are true, but I also believe this means that the instrument’s capabilities and performance must attain a sufficiently high standard to be of broad interest to the biology community. From this perspective, I believe the current method falls short on multiple fronts. Thus, my opinion is that the work is more suitable for a specialized journal.
## Main comments:

The device does not generate the trapping forces that biology labs would require for single-molecule studies and many cell stretching measurements. As clarified in the rebuttal, the maximum lateral trap stiffness attained here (see Figure 3: ~0.01 pN/um = 10-5 pN/nm at 40 mW) is several orders of magnitude lower than what is typical in bulk optical traps for similar input laser power. In addition, they estimate a maximum trapping force of 0.028 pN, which is at least three orders of magnitude lower than in a bulk optical trap. Importantly, as explained in Response #9 to Reviewer 2, scaling up the laser power does not seem to be a workable solution, as nonlinear effects appear to take hold. The authors estimate that the power plateaus around 50 mW, corresponding to a stiffness of 0.012 pN/um. (This also means that maximum trapping force would not increase appreciably beyond 0.03 pN). These low values are incompatible with many biophysical applications of interest.

In contrast, we note that the nanophotonic devices described in Ref. 11 (Ye et al. Nature Comm., 2022) a stiffness of 0.015 pN/nm and a force >20 pN could be attained, also 3 orders of magnitude higher than that reported here. In this case, Ye et al. are able to demonstrate single-molecule measurements stretching various DNA molecules and measurement protein-DNA interactions.

In their Response #6 to Reviewer 2, the authors also reveal that there is little confinement in the axial (z) direction. They write: “For this particular application, all the polystyrene beads in a given sample came to rest near the surface of the coverslip and there wasn’t a need for strong confinement in the z-direction.” This is an important point that should not have been omitted previously. If this statement is correct, then the bead is trapped only laterally and pushed against the surface of the coverslip, not as depicted in Fig. 4. In single-molecule measurements, the trapped bead should be suspended some distance above the coverslip; dragging a bead across it during a stretching cycle would lead to artifacts due to interactions with the surface. Again, this raises critical
questions on the compatibility of the device with a host of biophysical applications.
## Specific comments:

In comment 8 from my referee comments, I asked if the trap stiffness change with position as the trap is steered. The authors responded that in their experience, this remained “essentially constant” over the steering range, but it was unclear if this was determined from measurements or if this was the authors’ expectation. Presumably the transmission efficiency of the device varies as a function of wavelength. This variation should be measured and reported.

In Figure 3d, it seems that the trap stiffness vs laser power trend line does not extrapolate to the origin as it should. This is likely an artifact from measuring the variance in bead position over a finite time window (as the time increases, the variance will increase, leading to a lower estimate of the stiffness = kBT/<x^2>). This raises the question whether the authors are overestimating the trap stiffness. A more robust method to determine the trap stiffness is to measure the power spectral density in bead position (see for example Ye et al., Supplementary Figure 11).
## **Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):**

In their 2nd revision of the manuscript “Optical Tweezing of Microparticles and Cells Using SiliconPhotonics-Based Optical Phased Arrays” and in their rebuttal, Sneh et al. have responded to the latest reviewer comments. In particular, they have addressed two key criticisms that tempered my enthusiasm for the work. I had concerns over the low lateral trap stiffness given the laser power and the inability to scale it up due to two-photon absorption effects in silicon (Comment #2). In their rebuttal, the authors have clarified that the laser power emitted from the chip is actually 30x lower than the input power, and that the stiffness could in principle be increased with silicon nitride waveguides or by increasing the aperture size of the device. They convincingly argue that there is no fundamental limitation to increasing the lateral stiffness. I was also concerned over the low confinement in the axial (z) direction (Comment #3). The authors clarified that the trapped beads are offset from the surface, and that changes to the device aperture size could be used to increase confinement in the axial direction.
Overall, the main criticisms have been addressed appropriately. The manuscript is improved by these revisions and suitable for publication in Nature Communications.
One minor comment:

Response #3: The authors clarify that the trapped beads “rest near the bottom surface [of the coverslip]” but “are not in contact with either coverslip surface”. Could the authors estimate the distance between the bead and coverslip surface? Is this consistent with the 5-mm standoff distance in their device design? It would be useful to the readers to know what an effective working distance could be in practice with a sample chamber such as the one used in this study.
